meta.audience: Complete beginner; six focused hours/day; global career aspirations
meta.researchLimit: No current job posting sample was obtained; labor-market websites were blocked.

modules.title: Think in problems, evidence, and algorithms
modules.summary: Learn to turn an ambiguous wish into a small, testable computational problem before choosing a model.
modules.why: Engineering starts with deciding what success means. A correct program for the wrong objective is still a failure.
outcomes: Write measurable acceptance criteria
Trace a simple algorithm by hand
Separate observed facts from assumptions

project.title: The support-ticket decision brief
project.brief: Design a small system that routes fictional support tickets to billing, technical support, or a human reviewer. Begin with rules and a paper prototype.
deliverables: One-page problem statement with user, cost, constraints, and exclusions
Twenty invented tickets with expected routing and uncertainty cases
A flowchart or pseudocode procedure and manually checked trace table
rubric: Every acceptance criterion has an observable test
At least three ambiguous cases route safely to review
A simpler baseline is evaluated before proposing machine learning

pitfalls: Starting with a fashionable model instead of a user problem
Treating a proxy metric as the real-world goal
Confusing a plausible example with evidence

lessons.title: Define the decision before the solution
lessons.explain: A computer transforms an input into an output by following rules. Before writing those rules, identify the person who will use the output and the decision it should improve. An output such as a category is not itself a benefit; fewer wrongly routed tickets or less waiting might be. Separate the outcome you care about from the measurable proxy you can observe. Write constraints such as privacy, response time, and the option to ask a human. Include what the system will deliberately leave unresolved. This gives later experiments a target and prevents polished technology from hiding an undefined problem.
lessons.practice: Write two problem statements: routing a support ticket and predicting tomorrow’s shop demand. For each, name the user, available input, intended decision, error cost, and a no-software alternative.
lessons.deliverable: A comparison table containing two decisions and five acceptance criteria.
lessons.check: Why is “achieve 95% accuracy” insufficient as the whole requirement for a ticket router?
lessons.answer: It omits the population, label definition, baseline, relative error costs, operating constraints, and whether correct routing improves the user outcome. Accuracy can also hide failures on rare urgent cases.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50 introduction computational thinking and problem solving

lessons.title: Represent the world with explicit data
lessons.explain: Programs operate on representations of the world, not on the world directly. A ticket might become text, a timestamp, a language code, and a customer identifier. Each field needs a meaning, a unit or format, and a rule for missing values. The number zero is not interchangeable with unknown. An identifier written with digits is still usually a label rather than a quantity to average. Choosing a representation discards information, so record the assumptions that make that loss acceptable. Small examples are useful here: draw the records and ask whether another person could interpret each field without guessing.
lessons.practice: Create ten fictional ticket records on paper or in a plain text file. Define each field, three allowed categories, two missing-value cases, and a rule for time zones.
lessons.deliverable: A data dictionary and ten records that obey it.
lessons.check: Should a missing customer age be stored as zero? Explain one downstream consequence.
lessons.answer: Usually no. Zero is a real age and would bias averages or model behavior. Use an explicit missing value and document whether age is necessary at all.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50 data representation and information

lessons.title: Decompose a process into small algorithms
lessons.explain: An algorithm is a finite, precise process that transforms permitted inputs into the intended result. Break a task into steps whose inputs and outputs you can explain: validate a ticket, normalize its text, inspect routing rules, then return a category or ask for review. A branch chooses between paths; a loop repeats a step over a collection. An invariant is something that should remain true throughout the process, such as every ticket receiving exactly one final status. Trace the algorithm by hand before automating it. If a person cannot follow the rules consistently, a program will not remove the ambiguity.
lessons.practice: Write pseudocode for routing tickets that mention billing or login. Handle both keywords, neither keyword, empty text, and mixed capitalization. Trace it against the ten records.
lessons.deliverable: Pseudocode and a trace table showing every branch taken.
lessons.check: What should happen when both billing and login rules match, and why must the rule be explicit?
lessons.answer: The specification must define a priority, multiple-label behavior, or human review. Without an explicit policy the outcome depends on accidental code order rather than the intended decision.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50 algorithms conditions and loops

lessons.title: Estimate effort and search systematically
lessons.explain: An algorithm has both a meaning and a cost. To find an item in an unsorted list, you may need to inspect every item; doubling the list roughly doubles the worst-case checks. A sorted list allows binary search: each comparison discards half the remaining candidates, but sorting and maintaining order also cost work. Big-O describes how resource use grows, rather than the exact speed of one computer. For a small task, clear code is often the best choice. Still, estimating data size and repeated work helps you recognize when a perfectly correct approach becomes impractical.
lessons.practice: Find a target in 16 shuffled cards with linear search, then in 16 sorted cards with binary search. Count comparisons for a present and an absent target; predict counts for 1,024 cards.
lessons.deliverable: A comparison-count table and a paragraph explaining the sorting assumption.
lessons.check: How many times can you halve a candidate set of 1,024 items before at most one remains?
lessons.answer: Ten halvings, because 2 to the power 10 equals 1,024. Exact comparison counts depend on the implementation and whether the target exists.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50 algorithms searching and Big O

lessons.title: Build a paper baseline and falsify it
lessons.explain: A baseline is the simplest defensible system against which a more elaborate approach must earn its cost. For routing tickets, keyword rules or always choosing the common category are possible baselines, each with limitations. Test examples should include ordinary cases, boundary cases, and inputs designed to expose assumptions. A counterexample is valuable because it shows exactly where an apparently reasonable rule fails. Keep an error log with input, expected outcome, actual outcome, and likely cause. Your goal is not to defend the first design; it is to learn which additional information or capability the problem actually requires.
lessons.practice: Complete the support-ticket decision brief. Manually run the baseline over twenty tickets, including negation, ambiguous requests, and empty input. Propose one change supported by an observed failure.
lessons.deliverable: The decision brief, twenty-case evaluation, error log, and one justified revision.
lessons.check: A more complex router fixes two mistakes but creates three new mistakes. Is it necessarily worse?
lessons.answer: Not necessarily: compare the costs and severity of the changed errors on a representative evaluation set. Raw counts alone do not determine utility, but complexity needs evidence of benefit.

workedExample.title: Turn a vague request into a decision rule
workedExample.code:
INPUT: ticket text and an explicit customer-selected category
IF the category is "billing":
    send to the billing queue
ELSE IF the category is "technical":
    send to the technical queue
ELSE:
    ask a person to choose a queue
RECORD: chosen queue, human corrections, and waiting time
COMPARE: correction rate and waiting time against the current process
workedExample.expected: A billing ticket routes to billing. An unrecognized category goes to human triage. Success is measured against the existing process, not inferred from a working rule.
workedExample.explanation: This deliberately simple policy has inputs, branches, a fallback and observable outcomes. It establishes a useful non-ML baseline before collecting data or choosing a model. The rule can be tested without understanding Python. A fast route is not automatically a good route: corrections and waiting time expose different failure costs. The policy must also account for whose decision is recorded and when a human can intervene. Later, a learned classifier has to earn its added complexity on the same task.

assessment.question: A ticket classifier reaches 95% accuracy. Which missing fact is most important before claiming the product improved?
options: Whether it improves the actual routing decision against the current baseline and error costs.
The number of neural-network layers.
Whether the interface uses the newest framework.
Whether every ticket is automatically assigned without abstention.
assessment.explanation: A model score is evidence about a chosen measurement, not automatically about a useful outcome. Define the action, baseline, important errors and operational constraints first. A high overall score can coexist with costly failures on urgent tickets or no improvement over an existing rule. Abstaining for human triage can be part of a good policy.

connections.before: Start with an ordinary human decision that you can describe without technical vocabulary.
connections.after: The input, output, fallback and acceptance criteria become the contract for your first Python program.

modules.title: Python from a blank file
modules.summary: Read and write small Python programs, understand execution, and learn to debug with evidence.
modules.why: A model is embedded in ordinary software. Reliable control of values, conditions, loops, and errors is the first practical prerequisite.
outcomes: Run a script and explain each line
Use branches and loops safely
Turn an error message into a small reproducible example

project.title: A reliable study-time calculator
project.brief: Build a terminal program that converts a study goal and weekly availability into an estimated schedule while handling invalid input.
deliverables: A runnable Python script with clear prompts
Ten manually checked input/output examples
A short guide explaining assumptions and how to run it
rubric: Blank, zero, and negative availability are handled
Minutes and hours are not silently mixed
Estimate is labeled as a planning estimate rather than a promise

pitfalls: Copying code without tracing values
Using input strings as if they were numbers
Catching every exception and hiding the cause

lessons.title: Run code and inspect values
lessons.explain: Python executes instructions using values such as integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans. An expression computes a value; assignment gives a name to an object so later expressions can refer to it. The equals sign in assignment is an instruction, not a mathematical claim that remains true forever. Start with a terminal and a plain script so you can see where execution begins and how printed output relates to statements. Inspect types and intermediate values deliberately. Understanding what a short program does is more valuable than memorizing a long list of syntax that you cannot yet explain.
lessons.practice: Create a script that stores daily study minutes, days per week, and a goal in hours. Print the weekly total in both minutes and hours. Trace the value and type of each variable.
lessons.deliverable: One runnable script and a five-row value/type trace.
lessons.check: After x = 3; y = x; x = 5, what is y and why?
lessons.answer: y is 3. Assigning x = 5 rebinds x to a different integer object; it does not rewrite the earlier value referred to by y.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P functions variables and Python interpreter

lessons.title: Make decisions with conditions
lessons.explain: A conditional selects a block of instructions based on a boolean expression. Comparisons such as less than and equal to turn values into true or false; and, or, and not combine those results. Boundary cases deserve special attention because requirements often change exactly at zero, a threshold, or the edge of an allowed range. The order of conditions matters when several could be true. Write a decision table before the code, then choose branches that match the table. Keep input validation separate from the main calculation so an invalid value cannot quietly travel into a later formula.
lessons.practice: Accept a daily-minute value and classify it as invalid, short, standard, or long using ranges you document. Test zero and every range boundary, including one value immediately on each side.
lessons.deliverable: A decision table, conditional code, and boundary-case results.
lessons.check: Why does if minutes < 60 followed by elif minutes < 30 fail to select the second branch?
lessons.answer: Every value below 30 already satisfies the first branch, so the second is unreachable. Test narrower ranges first or express nonoverlapping conditions.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P conditionals boolean logic

lessons.title: Repeat work without losing control
lessons.explain: Loops express repeated computation without duplicating instructions. A for loop visits items from an iterable; a while loop repeats while a condition remains true. In either case, understand what changes on every iteration and what guarantees completion. An accumulator stores a running result such as total minutes. Off-by-one errors appear when the intended interval and the actual range disagree, so write down whether each endpoint is included. Trace a three-item example manually before trusting a larger run. When a loop seems stuck, inspect the condition and the variable that is supposed to make it become false.
lessons.practice: Ask for seven daily study totals, calculate the sum, and count days above a chosen target. Then write a retry loop that accepts only a positive weekly-hour value.
lessons.deliverable: A weekly summary program and a trace for three iterations.
lessons.check: What values does range(1, 4) produce, and how would you include 4?
lessons.answer: It produces 1, 2, and 3 because the stop endpoint is excluded. Use range(1, 5) to include 4.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P loops and iteration

lessons.title: Use errors as diagnostic evidence
lessons.explain: A failure message is a report about a specific operation, not a judgment about your ability. Read the final exception type and message, then locate the relevant line in the traceback. A syntax error prevents parsing; a runtime exception interrupts execution; a logic error can return a believable but incorrect result. Reduce the input and code until the failure is small enough to understand. Catch exceptions only where you can respond meaningfully, such as explaining an invalid number and requesting another entry. Assertions can document internal expectations, but validation of external input needs explicit handling because assertions may be disabled.
lessons.practice: Intentionally produce a syntax error, a division-by-zero error, and a unit-conversion logic error. Fix each and record what evidence identified the cause. Add focused handling for invalid numeric input.
lessons.deliverable: A debugging notebook with three minimal failures and their corrections.
lessons.check: Why is except Exception: pass a poor response to an unexpected failure?
lessons.answer: It hides the error and often leaves the program in an invalid state. Catch specific expected failures, explain or recover from them, and allow unexpected failures to remain visible.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P exceptions debugging Python

lessons.title: Ship your first small terminal program
lessons.explain: A useful program combines correct calculations with an understandable interaction. State what information the user should enter, validate it, and present a result with units. Rounding a displayed estimate is different from rounding intermediate values; premature rounding can accumulate error. A study schedule also depends on assumptions such as consistent availability and review time, so make those visible. Work from your earlier paper acceptance tests and add cases discovered during implementation. Finally, run the program from a new terminal using only your written instructions. This checks whether the artifact is usable independently of the session in which you created it.
lessons.practice: Finish the study-time calculator. Estimate weeks from goal hours and weekly study availability, include a configurable review allowance, and reject impossible inputs. Ask another person to follow the instructions or simulate a fresh user.
lessons.deliverable: A documented script with ten passing acceptance examples.
lessons.check: With 120 core hours, a 25% review allowance, and 15 hours/week, what is the estimate?
lessons.answer: The workload is 120 × 1.25 = 150 hours; 150 ÷ 15 = 10 weeks, assuming availability remains consistent.

workedExample.title: Trace values through a study-budget calculation
workedExample.code:
minutes_per_day = 360
days_per_week = 6
weekly_minutes = minutes_per_day * days_per_week
weekly_hours = weekly_minutes / 60
if weekly_hours >= 30:
    label = "intensive"
else:
    label = "lighter"
print("weekly_hours", weekly_hours)
print("pace", label)
workedExample.explanation: Assignment names a value; multiplication combines values; division converts units; the branch selects one label. The number 360 is minutes, not hours, so carrying the units through the expression is a useful correctness check. Python’s ordinary division returns a floating-point value, which explains 36.0. Change days_per_week to 4 and predict both printed lines before running. This is a complete executable program whose behavior can be traced line by line, without functions, packages or an editor extension.

assessment.question: After x = 3 and y = x, the program executes x = 7. What is y?
options: 7, because y permanently follows x.
3, because y was assigned the value referenced at that point.
An error, because two names cannot share a value.
A random value until the program is restarted.
assessment.explanation: Assignment is an action at a point in execution, not an algebraic relationship that continuously updates. The second assignment gives y the value currently referenced by x. Rebinding x later does not rebind y. Mutable objects introduce a separate aliasing issue, but this example uses immutable integers. Trace each statement instead of treating equals as a permanent equation.

connections.before: The decision rules in c01 become statements that execute in a specific order.
connections.after: Once you can trace values, functions and collections let you express the same logic without duplicating it.

modules.title: Functions, collections, and structured data
modules.summary: Organize programs around explicit inputs and outputs, and choose data structures that match the task.
modules.why: Data pipelines and models become maintainable when behavior is decomposed and state is controlled.
outcomes: Choose lists, dictionaries, sets, and tuples appropriately
Write focused functions with explicit contracts
Read and validate CSV and JSON data

project.title: A personal learning-log analyzer
project.brief: Read a fictional study log, validate entries, and summarize time by topic without losing or silently changing records.
deliverables: Functions for loading, validation, grouping, and reporting
Example CSV/JSON input and expected summary
Documented treatment of invalid and duplicated records
rubric: Each transformation has a clear input/output contract
Invalid records are counted and explained
Repeated runs on the same input produce the same report

pitfalls: Mutating a collection while iterating over it
Using mutable default arguments
Confusing a missing key with a valid zero value

lessons.title: Choose collections by their behavior
lessons.explain: A collection organizes multiple values according to useful rules. Lists preserve sequence and allow repeated items; tuples often represent fixed records; dictionaries map unique keys to values; sets represent distinct members. Choose based on the operations and meaning you need, rather than whichever syntax looks shortest. A list of study sessions can preserve chronology while a dictionary accumulates minutes per topic and a set records the topics encountered. Dictionary and set lookups are typically efficient, but their elements or keys must be hashable. Practice drawing the structures and tracing insertions before nesting them into complex shapes.
lessons.practice: Represent six study sessions as a list of dictionaries. Compute unique topics, minutes per topic, and the longest session. Include a repeated topic and a zero-minute entry.
lessons.deliverable: Three summaries and a written justification for each collection type.
lessons.check: What information disappears if the sequence ["math", "python", "math"] is converted to a set?
lessons.answer: Duplicate counts and sequence order are not preserved as sequence semantics. The set retains only distinct membership: math and python.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P lists dictionaries and Python data structures

lessons.title: Design functions as small contracts
lessons.explain: A function names a piece of behavior and makes its dependencies explicit through parameters. Its return value lets another part of the program use the result without depending on printed output. A good contract describes accepted inputs, returned output, and expected failures. Pure functions are especially easy to reason about because the same input gives the same output without changing external state. Not every operation can be pure: reading a file is inherently an interaction with the outside world. Keep that interaction near the edges, while placing calculations and validation rules in small functions you can exercise directly.
lessons.practice: Extract total_minutes, minutes_by_topic, and validate_session functions from the learning log. Make the calculation functions return data rather than print it. Write examples for valid and invalid inputs.
lessons.deliverable: Three functions with short contracts and example calls.
lessons.check: Why is returning a dictionary of totals more reusable than printing the totals inside the calculation?
lessons.answer: Callers can test, display, serialize, or further transform the returned data. Printing ties computation to one output channel and makes composition harder.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P functions return values and scope

lessons.title: Understand references and mutation
lessons.explain: Python names refer to objects. If two names refer to the same mutable list, modifying that list is visible through both names. Rebinding one name is different: it makes that name refer to another object. A shallow copy creates a new outer container but still shares nested objects, which matters for lists of dictionaries. Mutable default function arguments are created once when the function is defined, so accidental state can persist across calls. Use a None default and create a fresh container inside the function when appropriate. Draw arrows between names and objects to make these behaviors concrete.
lessons.practice: Build three small demonstrations: two names sharing a list, a shallow copy sharing a nested dictionary, and a function accidentally retaining a default list. Correct each design and explain the ownership rule.
lessons.deliverable: Before/after examples with object-reference diagrams.
lessons.check: After a = [{"x": 1}]; b = a.copy(); b[0]["x"] = 2, what is a[0]["x"]?
lessons.answer: It is 2. The outer lists are separate, but both still refer to the same inner dictionary. A shallow copy does not recursively duplicate nested objects.
lessons.videoQuery: Python tutorial objects mutability and default arguments

lessons.title: Read data with explicit formats
lessons.explain: A file format is a contract between the program that writes data and the program that reads it. CSV represents rows and columns but leaves many type rules to you; JSON represents nested values with defined basic types. Text also has an encoding, commonly UTF-8. Use standard parsing libraries rather than splitting CSV on commas, because quoted fields may contain commas or newlines. A context manager closes a file reliably even when an exception occurs. After parsing, validate the schema: successful parsing does not mean that required fields exist, values have suitable types, or the data makes sense.
lessons.practice: Create a CSV learning log with a quoted comma in a topic, a missing duration, and non-ASCII text. Load it using the csv module, validate records, and export accepted records as UTF-8 JSON.
lessons.deliverable: Input CSV, output JSON, and a rejection report with row numbers.
lessons.check: Why can line.split(",") misread a valid CSV record?
lessons.answer: A comma can occur inside a quoted field, and quoting/escaping rules determine whether it is a separator. A CSV parser implements those rules; naive splitting does not.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P file I O csv json Python

lessons.title: Compose a small data-processing pipeline
lessons.explain: A pipeline connects transformations while preserving a clear account of what happened to the data. Loading, validation, grouping, and reporting are distinct responsibilities; each can be understood and tested separately. Define whether invalid records stop the run or enter a rejection report, and make the choice appropriate to the consequences. Determinism means the same accepted input and settings lead to the same result, including stable output ordering when it matters. Record counts provide a simple conservation check: loaded records should equal accepted plus rejected records. This habit scales from a tiny learning log to much larger machine-learning data workflows.
lessons.practice: Finish the learning-log analyzer. Include an explicit duplicate policy, stable topic ordering, a row-count conservation check, and a summary of accepted/rejected records. Verify it against hand-calculated totals.
lessons.deliverable: The complete analyzer and a reproducible example report.
lessons.check: If 12 rows are loaded, 2 rejected, and 3 accepted duplicates intentionally removed, how many records contribute to the final report?
lessons.answer: Seven records contribute. The accounting must distinguish rejected records from accepted records removed under the duplicate policy: 12 = 2 + 3 + 7.

workedExample.title: Aggregate records without losing repeated observations
workedExample.explanation: A list preserves the three observations, including repeated Python work. A dictionary represents a different grain: one accumulated value per topic. The function makes that transformation explicit and rejects a value that violates the input contract. Using a set of records before summing could silently remove legitimate repeats; overwriting the dictionary value would lose earlier sessions. The choice of collection follows the meaning of the data and the operations needed, not a preference for compact syntax.

assessment.question: Two identical purchases occur at different times. Why can converting purchase rows to a set before aggregation be wrong?
options: Sets always sort monetary values incorrectly.
Dictionaries cannot contain numbers.
It may erase a legitimate repeated event because equality of values is not identity of events.
All duplicate-looking records must always be retained regardless of provenance.
assessment.explanation: Deduplication is a claim about event identity. Two rows with the same visible values may be two real events, while two distinct-looking rows may be retransmissions of one event. Use stable event identifiers and a documented policy. Collections do not decide the data’s meaning; the programmer must establish the grain and identity rules before choosing an operation.

connections.before: Python expressions and loops are now organized around explicit input and output contracts.
connections.after: These contracts become tests in c04 and data-grain constraints in c06.

modules.title: Engineering habits: Git, tests, and reproducibility
modules.summary: Make small programs recoverable, testable, reviewable, and reproducible on another machine.
modules.why: Professional engineering depends on trustworthy changes, not just code that worked once in one session.
outcomes: Use commits and diffs to explain changes
Create focused automated tests
Reproduce a small project in an isolated environment

project.title: A reproducible learning-log repository
project.brief: Package the analyzer as a small repository with tests, explicit dependencies, and a repeatable command-line workflow.
deliverables: README with installation and run commands
Focused tests for calculation and validation
A small commit history that separates behavior changes
Dependency/version record and an example input
rubric: A clean environment reproduces the documented report
Tests catch a deliberately introduced calculation bug
No credentials, personal data, or generated environments are committed

pitfalls: Committing secrets or large generated folders
Tests that reproduce implementation without checking behavior
Changing several unrelated behaviors in one commit

lessons.title: Use the shell and understand project boundaries
lessons.explain: The shell launches programs and connects their input and output. A command runs in a working directory; relative paths are interpreted from there, while absolute paths identify a location directly. Standard output carries normal results, standard error carries diagnostics, and an exit code communicates success or failure to other programs. Learn a small, safe vocabulary for listing files, changing directories, inspecting text, and running scripts. Before a command that changes or removes files, confirm the target path and understand its effect. Knowing the execution context prevents many apparent Python problems that are actually missing files, wrong directories, or wrong interpreters.
lessons.practice: Run the analyzer from its project directory and from another directory using an explicit input path. Inspect successful and failing exit codes. Write down the directory and interpreter assumptions.
lessons.deliverable: A command transcript and a short project-path diagram.
lessons.check: Why can a script that opens data.csv succeed in one terminal and fail in another?
lessons.answer: A relative path is resolved against the process working directory, which may differ between terminals. Use an explicit input path or deliberately resolve paths relative to a known project location.
lessons.videoQuery: MIT missing semester shell tools and scripting

lessons.title: Version changes with Git
lessons.explain: Git records snapshots of tracked files so changes can be inspected, compared, and recovered. The working tree is your editable copy; staging selects the next snapshot; a commit records it with an explanation. A branch is a movable reference to a line of commits, not a second folder by itself. Read the diff before committing, and keep each change focused enough to describe in one sentence. Ignored files still exist locally but are excluded from routine tracking; this is useful for generated environments and caches. Credentials belong in secure configuration, and adding them to ignore rules after committing does not erase their history.
lessons.practice: Initialize or use a practice repository for the analyzer. Commit a working baseline, make one validation improvement, inspect the diff, and commit it separately. Create a branch and practice resolving a small intentional conflict on disposable text.
lessons.deliverable: Three understandable commits and a .gitignore appropriate to the project.
lessons.check: Does deleting a secret from the latest file remove it from Git history?
lessons.answer: No. Earlier commits can still contain it. Exposed credentials need revocation or rotation, followed by an appropriate history-cleanup procedure when necessary.
lessons.videoQuery: Pro Git recording changes and branching basics

lessons.title: Test behavior at useful boundaries
lessons.explain: A test supplies controlled input and checks an observable property of the result. Start with calculations and validation rules because they can run quickly without files or networks. Include an ordinary case, a boundary case, and a failure case chosen from the function’s contract. A regression test captures a bug so the same behavior cannot silently return. The strongest evidence that a test matters is that it fails when the behavior is intentionally broken. Avoid asserting every internal implementation detail; useful tests allow refactoring while preserving the promise made to users. Keep test data small enough that expected results can be checked by hand.
lessons.practice: Write tests for total minutes, grouping, invalid negative duration, and a missing field. Introduce a temporary off-by-one or double-counting bug, confirm a relevant test fails, then restore the correct code.
lessons.deliverable: A focused automated suite and evidence of one meaningful failure.
lessons.check: Why can 100% line coverage still coexist with incorrect behavior?
lessons.answer: Executing every line does not guarantee that tests check the right outputs, edge cases, or requirements. Coverage measures execution, not the strength or completeness of assertions.
lessons.videoQuery: CS50P unit tests pytest

lessons.title: Isolate dependencies and record assumptions
lessons.explain: A program depends on more than its source code: the Python version, installed libraries, configuration, and input data can change its behavior. A virtual environment isolates Python packages for a project so unrelated work does not silently alter them. Record necessary dependencies and use the repository’s supported lock or version mechanism when one exists. Keep configuration separate from code, and never copy secrets into a dependency file or README. Reproducibility also requires recording data and execution instructions. For this small project, prefer the standard library where it suffices; adding a package creates a maintenance obligation that should have a clear benefit.
lessons.practice: Create an isolated environment, install only the test tool if needed, record the Python/dependency versions, and run the tests with explicit commands. Recreate the environment in a second local directory.
lessons.deliverable: A version record and installation instructions verified in a fresh environment.
lessons.check: Does pinning library versions guarantee identical model results across all machines?
lessons.answer: No. Hardware, low-level libraries, nondeterministic algorithms, seeds, data, and configuration can also affect results. Pins are one component of reproducibility, not a complete guarantee.
lessons.videoQuery: Python tutorial virtual environments and packages

lessons.title: Make a project usable by another person
lessons.explain: A repository is an interface for future users and maintainers. Its README should state the purpose, prerequisites, installation steps, one working example, expected output, and known limitations. A command-line entry point should communicate invalid input clearly and return a nonzero exit status when it cannot complete the requested work. Logs should explain useful events without leaking sensitive content. The final test is a clean reproduction using only the written instructions, not your memory of hidden setup steps. Documenting a small project well is practice for explaining larger systems whose data, training, deployment, and operational assumptions are much harder to reconstruct.
lessons.practice: Finish the reproducible analyzer repository. Run its documented example from a new environment, verify the expected output, and write a short change review explaining one design choice and one limitation.
lessons.deliverable: A clean reproduction report and a reviewer-ready repository.
lessons.check: What should a script return when its input file is missing, and what should the user see?
lessons.answer: It should return a nonzero exit code and a concise diagnostic identifying the missing input and how to provide a valid path, without hiding the failure behind an empty success result.

workedExample.title: Make edge cases executable evidence
workedExample.explanation: The normal case checks the calculation, the single-item case checks a boundary, and the empty case checks the failure contract. A useful test can fail when behavior is wrong; merely executing a function does not establish its result. The test also makes an API decision visible: an empty mean is an explicit error, not an invented zero. In a project, put these cases in the test runner and run them from a clean environment. Version control should preserve the implementation, tests and explanation of the change together.

assessment.question: A test imports a module and exits successfully without checking a result. What has it established?
options: Every function in the module is correct.
That the module has no security or performance defects.
That the package is reproducible on every machine.
Only that import succeeded in that environment; behavior still needs assertions.
assessment.explanation: Importing exercises module loading and top-level code. It can catch missing dependencies or syntax problems, but it does not validate uncalled functions or expected outputs. A behavioral test supplies representative inputs, checks observable results and includes a meaningful failure condition. Reproducibility also requires the runtime, dependency versions, configuration and inputs to be controlled.

connections.before: Functions from c03 expose behavior that can be checked independently.
connections.after: The same habit scales to preprocessing, training, APIs and deployment smoke tests.

modules.title: Numerical computing with arrays
modules.summary: Build intuition for array shapes, vectorized calculations, floating-point limits, and reproducible numerical work.
modules.why: Most machine-learning calculations operate on batches of numbers; shape and unit errors can silently corrupt otherwise valid code.
outcomes: Track array shapes through transformations
Use broadcasting deliberately
Recognize numerical instability and compare against a simple reference

project.title: A transparent numerical data profiler
project.brief: Compute column summaries and standardized features from a small numeric dataset, with explicit handling of missing and constant columns.
deliverables: Array-based implementation and a loop-based reference
Shape and dtype annotations for intermediate values
Tests for missing values, constant columns, and extreme magnitudes
rubric: Vectorized and reference outputs agree within justified tolerance
No divide-by-zero for constant features
Memory use and copying behavior are explained

pitfalls: Broadcasting into the wrong shape without noticing
Comparing floating-point results with exact equality
Standardizing with statistics from future evaluation data

lessons.title: Treat shape as part of the type
lessons.explain: An array stores values together with a shape and a numeric type. A two-dimensional table might have shape (samples, features), while a vector of labels has one value per sample. The meaning of each axis is a contract you must maintain through every operation. Reducing along an axis removes or collapses that dimension: a column mean summarizes samples, whereas a row mean summarizes features within one sample. The dtype controls representation, precision, and memory, so integers and floating-point values are not interchangeable in every calculation. Annotate shapes next to code until you can predict them before running the program.
lessons.practice: Create a 4-by-3 array of fictional measurements. Compute per-column and per-row sums, inspect dtypes, and explain the shape of every result. Compare indexing a column with preserving it as a two-dimensional slice.
lessons.deliverable: An annotated shape table and executable NumPy examples.
lessons.check: For X with shape (4, 3), what is the shape of X.mean(axis=0)?
lessons.answer: It is (3,), one mean for each feature after reducing the four samples. With keepdims=True it is (1, 3).
lessons.videoQuery: NumPy absolute beginners array shape and axes

lessons.title: Vectorize without hiding the mathematics
lessons.explain: Vectorization expresses a calculation over whole arrays rather than a Python loop, allowing optimized numerical routines to do the repeated work. Broadcasting aligns dimensions from the right and permits dimensions of size one to expand conceptually. That convenience is also a source of subtle mistakes: a column vector and a one-dimensional vector can combine into a matrix when you intended pairwise subtraction. Write the scalar formula first, then the expected input and output shapes, and only then the vectorized expression. Keep a tiny loop-based implementation as a reference when introducing a new numerical calculation.
lessons.practice: Compute squared differences between predicted and observed values with a loop and with arrays. Deliberately compare shapes (5,) and (5, 1), observe the unexpected result, and correct it.
lessons.deliverable: Matching reference/vectorized calculations plus a documented broadcasting failure.
lessons.check: What shape results from subtracting an array shaped (5,) from one shaped (5, 1)?
lessons.answer: The result has shape (5, 5): trailing dimensions 1 and 5 broadcast to 5, and the missing leading dimension broadcasts against 5. Reshape deliberately for pairwise comparison.
lessons.videoQuery: NumPy broadcasting user guide examples

lessons.title: Index data and understand views
lessons.explain: Indexing selects which values participate in a calculation. Boolean masks express conditions such as finite measurements or values above a threshold, while slices select regular ranges. NumPy basic slicing often returns a view that shares the underlying memory; changing that view can change the original array. Advanced indexing typically creates a copy, so apparently similar selections can have different mutation behavior. Treat ownership as an explicit design choice, especially when cleaning data. Preserve raw inputs and create deliberate transformed outputs. Record how many rows each filter removes so a convenient mask does not silently change the population you intend to study.
lessons.practice: Create a measurement array with one invalid row. Filter it with a boolean mask, compare a slice with an explicit copy, and demonstrate which edits affect the original. Log row counts before and after filtering.
lessons.deliverable: A safe filtering function and a view/copy demonstration.
lessons.check: Why can x[1:3] += 10 change x itself?
lessons.answer: The basic slice is usually a view sharing x’s memory, so in-place modification changes the underlying values. Use an explicit copy when independent ownership is required.
lessons.videoQuery: NumPy copies views and indexing

lessons.title: Respect floating-point limits
lessons.explain: Floating-point numbers represent a finite set of values, so many decimal fractions and arithmetic results are approximations. Reordering operations can change rounding, and subtracting nearly equal large numbers can lose meaningful precision. Exponentials can overflow for large inputs or underflow for very negative inputs. Compare numerical results using a justified absolute and relative tolerance rather than assuming exact equality. The tolerance should reflect the scale and purpose of the calculation. Stable reformulations often matter more than simply choosing a larger dtype; later, shifting logits before a softmax will be an example of preserving the same mathematics while improving numerical behavior.
lessons.practice: Explore 0.1 + 0.2, a large-plus-small sum, and exponentials of large values. Use numpy.isclose with documented tolerances, and compare a naive sum with a higher-precision or carefully ordered reference.
lessons.deliverable: Three numerical failure examples and a short tolerance policy.
lessons.check: Why is an absolute tolerance alone unsuitable when comparing both values near zero and values near one billion?
lessons.answer: A fixed absolute error has very different significance at different scales. Relative tolerance handles proportional error for large values, while an absolute term remains necessary near zero.
lessons.videoQuery: NumPy floating point error handling and numerical precision

lessons.title: Build and verify a numerical profiler
lessons.explain: A profiler summarizes data while making assumptions visible. For a numeric column, count valid observations before computing a mean or spread; otherwise a missing-value policy can be mistaken for a property of the population. Standardization subtracts a mean and divides by a scale so features can be compared numerically, but a constant column has zero scale and needs an explicit policy. Preserve the fitted statistics separately from transformed data because future inputs must use the same transformation. Verify the implementation on tiny cases with known answers before considering performance. Correctness, transparency, and stable behavior matter more than a short expression.
lessons.practice: Complete the numerical profiler with counts, means, population standard deviations, and standardized values. Treat constant columns explicitly, preserve input arrays, and compare results against a loop implementation on a 5-by-3 example.
lessons.deliverable: Profiler code, a hand-checked example, and numerical edge-case tests.
lessons.check: If a column is [2, 2, 2], why does ordinary z-score standardization fail and what is one defensible policy?
lessons.answer: Its standard deviation is zero, so division is undefined. A documented policy can map the constant column to zeros or remove it, while preserving metadata about the choice.

workedExample.title: Let shapes explain broadcasting
workedExample.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
row_totals = X.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
normalized = X / row_totals
print("X", X.shape)
print("row_totals", row_totals.shape)
print(np.round(normalized, 3))
assert np.allclose(normalized.sum(axis=1), 1)
workedExample.explanation: Reducing across axis 1 sums the features within each row. Keeping the dimension produces shape (2, 1), so division broadcasts each row’s own total across its two columns. Without keepdims, a shape-(2,) array aligns with the last axis and can silently normalize columns by the wrong values when the dimensions happen to match. A shape annotation and the row-sum invariant explain the operation more reliably than a successful execution. Real normalization also needs an explicit policy for zero totals.

assessment.question: For X with shape (10, 3), what shape should per-row totals have to divide every row by its own total?
options: (10, 1), so each total broadcasts across its row.
(3,), because there are three features.
(1, 10), because reductions always produce row vectors.
(10, 3, 1), because division adds a new axis.
assessment.explanation: Broadcasting compares dimensions from the right. A (10, 1) array matches the ten rows and expands its singleton feature dimension to three. A (10,) array does not align with a (10, 3) matrix in the intended way. Write the meaning and size of each axis before operating, and verify an invariant such as row sums equal to one.

connections.before: Collection operations become explicit shape-aware numerical transformations.
connections.after: Linear algebra, neural-network batches and feature pipelines all rely on these same axis contracts.

modules.title: Data modeling and SQL
modules.summary: Understand relational data, query it precisely, and prevent joins or time semantics from silently changing the question.
modules.why: Useful ML starts with trustworthy data extraction; many expensive modeling failures originate in an incorrect query.
outcomes: Write filters, aggregations, and joins
State the grain and keys of a dataset
Audit missingness, duplication, and event-time semantics

project.title: A trustworthy subscription analytics dataset
project.brief: Use a small SQLite database of fictional customers, subscriptions, and events to produce a customer-level analysis table.
deliverables: Schema with primary and foreign-key meanings
Queries for revenue, active customers, and event counts
Join-cardinality and row-count checks
A data dictionary defining the observation window
rubric: Every output table has an explicit grain
Joins do not multiply revenue silently
Missing and zero values remain semantically distinct

pitfalls: Joining tables without checking one-to-many cardinality
Using future events in a historical feature
Averaging averages without correct weighting

lessons.title: Define tables, keys, and grain
lessons.explain: A relational table represents facts at a particular grain: one row per customer, per subscription, or per event. A primary key identifies a row uniquely; a foreign key refers to a row in another table. These relationships let you separate entities instead of copying the same facts into many places. Before querying, write a sentence beginning “one row means.” Many data errors occur when tables with different grains are combined as if they were interchangeable. Constraints express expectations such as uniqueness and required values, while a data dictionary explains the meaning that a database cannot infer from a column name.
lessons.practice: Design three SQLite tables for customers, subscriptions, and events. Insert a tiny fictional dataset with two subscriptions for one customer and multiple events per subscription. State each table’s grain and keys.
lessons.deliverable: Schema, sample records, and a relationship diagram.
lessons.check: Why is customer_id usually not a valid primary key for an events table?
lessons.answer: One customer can produce multiple events, so customer_id is not unique at event grain. Use a unique event identifier and keep customer_id as a relationship to the customer table.
lessons.videoQuery: PostgreSQL tutorial relational concepts and tables

lessons.title: Select, filter, and aggregate deliberately
lessons.explain: A query describes the result you want rather than the exact loop used to obtain it. Filtering chooses rows; grouping partitions them; aggregate functions summarize each group. WHERE filters rows before aggregation, while HAVING filters groups after aggregate values exist. NULL represents an absent or unknown value and follows three-valued logic, so equality comparisons do not behave like ordinary values. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column. Predict the result on a small table before running the query; this makes the logical order and missing-value behavior visible.
lessons.practice: Write queries for active subscriptions, revenue by plan, and customers with at least two events. Add one NULL amount and compare COUNT(*), COUNT(amount), and SUM(amount). Explain every difference.
lessons.deliverable: Five queries with hand-calculated expected result tables.
lessons.check: Why does WHERE amount = NULL fail to select missing amounts?
lessons.answer: Comparisons with NULL yield unknown rather than true. Use amount IS NULL to test for missingness explicitly.
lessons.videoQuery: PostgreSQL SELECT GROUP BY aggregate functions NULL

lessons.title: Join without multiplying facts
lessons.explain: A join combines rows that satisfy a relationship. An inner join keeps matches; a left join also retains unmatched rows from the left table, filling right-side fields with NULL. The number of matching rows matters: joining one subscription payment to five events can repeat the payment five times. Summing after that join can inflate revenue even though the SQL runs successfully. State the expected cardinality before joining, test key uniqueness, and compare row counts and totals afterward. Often the correct solution is to aggregate each source to the intended grain before combining them.
lessons.practice: Join subscriptions to events and demonstrate an inflated revenue total. Correct the query by aggregating events per subscription first. Include a subscription with no events and compare inner versus left joins.
lessons.deliverable: A failing query, corrected query, and cardinality audit.
lessons.check: A $10 subscription joins to three event rows. What revenue appears if you sum the joined amount, and how can you avoid it?
lessons.answer: It appears as $30. Aggregate events to one row per subscription before joining, or calculate revenue from the subscription-grain table without duplicating payments.
lessons.videoQuery: PostgreSQL joins table expressions cardinality

lessons.title: Reason about time and missing observations
lessons.explain: An event can have several timestamps: when it occurred, when it was recorded, and when it became available to your system. Those times answer different questions. A historical dataset must use only information available at the decision time; otherwise later events can leak into earlier predictions. Observation windows also affect interpretation: a new customer has had less opportunity to produce events than a long-standing customer. Missing events may mean inactivity, delayed ingestion, or incomplete instrumentation. Define the window, time zone, and late-arrival policy explicitly so an apparent behavioral signal does not merely reflect how the data was collected.
lessons.practice: Create events with event_time and recorded_time, including one delayed record. Build a customer summary as of a fixed cutoff using only records available then. Compare it with an unrestricted query.
lessons.deliverable: Two as-of queries and a note identifying which records were excluded and why.
lessons.check: An event occurred Monday but was ingested Wednesday. Can a Tuesday historical prediction use it?
lessons.answer: Only if the real system had access to the event by Tuesday through a valid source. If the dataset records Wednesday availability, using it in Tuesday features creates availability leakage.
lessons.videoQuery: Google machine learning data leakage time dependent data

lessons.title: Publish an auditable analysis table
lessons.explain: An analysis table should arrive with enough context to be trusted and reproduced. Document its grain, keys, population, observation window, source tables, and transformation logic. Quality checks should target meaningful failures: duplicate keys, impossible values, unexpected missingness, and totals that no longer reconcile to source data. These checks do not prove all data are correct, but they make important assumptions executable. Keep excluded records and reasons visible rather than silently cleaning until a result looks plausible. A compact, auditable dataset is a stronger foundation for modeling than a large table whose joins and temporal meaning nobody can explain.
lessons.practice: Complete the subscription analytics dataset. Produce one row per customer with revenue and event counts as of a cutoff, add uniqueness and reconciliation checks, and document the treatment of new customers and late events.
lessons.deliverable: SQL scripts, an output table, and a data contract with checks.
lessons.check: What two checks would quickly expose an accidental one-to-many join in a customer-level table?
lessons.answer: Check uniqueness of customer_id and compare the row count with the intended customer population. Reconcile additive measures such as revenue to their source-grain totals as an additional safeguard.

workedExample.title: Aggregate at the intended relational grain
workedExample.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ada'), (2, 'Bo');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1, 12), (11, 1, 18), (12, 2, 7);
""")
rows = con.execute("""
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount)
FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id
""").fetchall()
print(rows)
con.close()
workedExample.explanation: The customers table has one row per customer; orders has one row per order. Joining them expands Ada into two rows before grouping returns one row per customer. That expansion is intended here. Joining another one-to-many table, such as support events, before summing could multiply each order and inflate revenue. Inspect row counts and keys around joins. SQLite makes the mechanism runnable without a server; transaction behavior, types and syntax must still be checked when moving to another database.

assessment.question: A customer has two orders and three support events. Joining both child tables to the customer produces how many rows for that customer before grouping?
options: 2 rows: joins preserve the left table’s order count.
6 rows: each order pairs with each event unless the join adds another restriction.
3 rows: the larger child table wins.
1 row: the primary key automatically aggregates children.
assessment.explanation: A join returns combinations satisfying its condition. With both child tables joined only on customer ID, two orders each match three events, producing six rows. Summing order amounts at that point repeats each order three times. Aggregate each child to the required grain first, or use a query structure that avoids the unintended multiplication.

connections.before: Structured records from c03 acquire explicit keys, relationships and row meanings.
connections.after: Leakage audits and data pipelines depend on preserving those meanings across transformations.

modules.title: Functions, algebra, and change
modules.summary: Build the mathematical language needed to describe models, losses, and optimization from simple numerical examples.
modules.why: Mathematics becomes useful when each symbol describes a quantity, transformation, or rate you can compute and check.
outcomes: Manipulate functions and units
Interpret derivatives as local rates of change
Use gradients to improve a simple objective

project.title: Gradient descent you can inspect
project.brief: Fit a line to a tiny dataset using an explicitly written squared-error objective and gradient descent, then compare against a known solution.
deliverables: A derivation with each symbol defined
A numerical gradient check
A plot or table of loss during optimization
An explanation of learning-rate failures
rubric: Analytic and finite-difference gradients agree locally
Loss decreases with an appropriate step size
The learner can explain why an excessive step diverges

pitfalls: Memorizing derivative rules without interpreting quantities
Mixing units inside an equation
Assuming gradient descent always finds a global optimum

lessons.title: Use algebra to describe relationships
lessons.explain: Algebra replaces particular numbers with symbols so one relationship can describe many cases. A variable needs a meaning and, when appropriate, a unit. An equation states that two expressions have equal values under stated conditions; solving it means finding values that satisfy that relationship. Units provide a powerful error check: adding hours to dollars is meaningless unless a conversion is defined. Start with familiar quantities such as distance, speed, and time, then describe a prediction as a weighted combination of inputs. Rearranging an equation is not a separate ritual; it is a way to answer a different question about the same relationship.
lessons.practice: Derive total study weeks from hours per session, sessions per week, and total work. Then write a linear price model with a fixed fee and per-unit cost. Solve three numerical examples and check units.
lessons.deliverable: Two symbolic formulas, unit annotations, and checked examples.
lessons.check: For cost = 12 + 3 × units, how many units can be purchased with a total cost of 30?
lessons.answer: Subtract the fixed fee to get 18 = 3 × units, then divide by 3: units = 6. The fixed fee and total cost must use the same currency.
lessons.videoQuery: Khan Academy algebra linear equations functions

lessons.title: Understand functions and composition
lessons.explain: A function maps an allowed input to an output according to a rule. Its domain states which inputs are permitted, while its range describes possible outputs. Composition applies one transformation after another, such as normalizing a value and then computing a score. Exponentials model multiplicative growth; logarithms invert exponentials and turn products into sums, which will later make probability calculations easier to optimize. A graph, a formula, and a small input-output table are complementary descriptions of the same function. Always inspect behavior near boundaries and extreme inputs rather than relying on a graph’s convenient visible window.
lessons.practice: Tabulate and plot a linear function, a square, an exponential, and a logarithm over appropriate domains. Compose two simple functions in both orders and identify when the results differ.
lessons.deliverable: Four function sketches and a composition comparison.
lessons.check: If f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x squared, are f(g(2)) and g(f(2)) equal?
lessons.answer: No. f(g(2))=f(4)=9, while g(f(2))=g(5)=25. Composition order changes the transformation.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown essence of calculus functions and composition

lessons.title: Interpret derivatives as local sensitivity
lessons.explain: A derivative describes how sensitively a function’s output changes near a particular input. For a straight line the slope is constant; for a curve it depends on location. A finite difference approximates the derivative by comparing nearby function values, while the derivative describes the limiting local rate. Very large finite-difference steps blur local behavior, and extremely small steps can amplify floating-point error. Connect the symbol to a concrete question: if a model parameter increases slightly, does the loss rise or fall, and by how much? This interpretation makes derivatives useful before you learn a large catalog of rules.
lessons.practice: For f(x)=x cubed, estimate the derivative at x=3 with central differences [f(3+h)−f(3−h)]/(2h), using h=1, 0.1, 0.01, 1e-5, 1e-8 and 1e-12. Compare with 27. Derive why the exact-arithmetic approximation is 27+h squared. Then repeat for x squared: its central difference is exactly 6 in exact arithmetic, so large-h truncation error is absent for this special case. Distinguish truncation error from floating-point cancellation.
lessons.deliverable: A finite-difference error table for cubic and quadratic functions, with a derivation of the cubic h-squared truncation term and a note about floating-point cancellation.
lessons.check: What is the derivative of x squared at x=3, and what does it predict for a small positive change in x?
lessons.answer: The derivative is 2x, so it is 6. A sufficiently small change Δx produces an approximate output change of 6Δx, with higher-order error.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown derivative intuition essence of calculus

lessons.title: Follow dependencies with the chain rule
lessons.explain: A model often composes many simple operations, and the chain rule tracks how a change travels through them. If an output depends on an intermediate value that depends on a parameter, multiply the local rates along that path. When several paths contribute, add their effects. A partial derivative changes one input while holding the others fixed; collecting these derivatives gives a gradient. Draw a computational graph for a simple prediction and loss before calculating derivatives. Each node then has a local meaning, and the final gradient becomes an accounting of influence rather than an opaque symbolic expression.
lessons.practice: For prediction yhat=w*x+b and loss (yhat-y) squared, draw the graph and derive derivatives with respect to w and b. Check both with finite differences on one numeric example.
lessons.deliverable: A computational graph, two derivative formulas, and numerical checks.
lessons.check: For x=2, y=5, w=1, b=0, what are the derivatives of squared error with respect to w and b?
lessons.answer: The residual is -3. dL/dw=2×(-3)×2=-12 and dL/db=2×(-3)=-6.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown chain rule and computational graphs

lessons.title: Optimize an objective and inspect failure
lessons.explain: Optimization chooses parameters that improve a defined objective. Gradient descent takes a small step opposite the gradient because that direction locally reduces a differentiable function most rapidly under the usual Euclidean geometry. The step size controls how far the local approximation is trusted. Too small can be slow; too large can overshoot or diverge. A decreasing training objective is evidence about the optimization procedure, not proof that the model generalizes or solves the right problem. Keep those questions separate. For a simple convex quadratic, compare the iterative result with a known solution so you can diagnose the algorithm rather than guessing from a plot.
lessons.practice: Fit a line to five synthetic points with gradient descent. Log parameters and mean squared error, compare three learning rates, and verify the final predictions against a known generating line or least-squares reference.
lessons.deliverable: An optimization report with one successful and one divergent run.
lessons.check: For L(w)=w squared and update w_new=w-η(2w), what happens with η=1.5?
lessons.answer: The update is w_new=-2w, so the magnitude doubles at each step unless w starts at zero. The loss diverges because the step size is too large.

workedExample.title: Separate truncation error from floating-point error
workedExample.code:
def f(x):
    return x ** 3
x = 3.0
exact = 3 * x ** 2
for h in (1.0, 0.1, 0.01):
    estimate = (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)
    error = estimate - exact
    print(f"h={h:.2f} derivative={estimate:.4f} error={error:.4f}")
workedExample.expected:
h=1.00 derivative=28.0000 error=1.0000
h=0.10 derivative=27.0100 error=0.0100
h=0.01 derivative=27.0001 error=0.0001
workedExample.explanation: Expanding (x+h)³ and (x−h)³ shows that their central difference is 3x²+h². The h² term is truncation error: halving h reduces this term by a factor of four in exact arithmetic. Extremely small h can instead expose subtraction and rounding error, so smaller is not unconditionally better. A quadratic is a useful contrast because its central difference is exact in exact arithmetic. This derivation connects a numerical table to the derivative’s local-sensitivity meaning instead of treating the approximation as a magic formula.

assessment.question: Why can making a finite-difference step extremely small eventually make the numerical derivative worse?
options: The mathematical derivative changes when the step changes.
Small steps always change a convex function into a nonconvex one.
Subtracting nearly equal floating-point values can lose significant digits.
Central differences never approximate derivatives.
assessment.explanation: A finite-difference estimate has both approximation error and floating-point error. Smaller steps usually reduce truncation error, but the numerator becomes a difference between nearly equal rounded values. Dividing that noisy difference by a tiny step can amplify numerical error. Compare several step sizes and use a derived analytic gradient when available, rather than assuming an arbitrarily small step is best.

connections.before: Python arithmetic and function composition now describe local changes in an objective.
connections.after: Backpropagation uses the chain rule to combine these local sensitivities across a model.

modules.title: Linear algebra as geometry and computation
modules.summary: Understand vectors, matrices, projections, and rank through transformations you can visualize and implement.
modules.why: Linear models, embeddings, neural networks, and dimensionality reduction all reuse the same small set of linear-algebra ideas.
outcomes: Interpret dot products and matrix multiplication
Explain projections and least squares
Recognize rank, conditioning, and dimensionality limits

project.title: A geometric least-squares laboratory
project.brief: Fit and visualize a small linear system, compare exact and noisy cases, and diagnose dependent features.
deliverables: Shape-checked matrix computations
A least-squares solution and residual analysis
A dependent-feature example with rank discussion
An explanation of why a stable solver is preferred to explicit inversion
rubric: Matrix dimensions are predicted before execution
Residual orthogonality is checked within tolerance
Ill-conditioned cases are identified without treating numerical output as certainty

pitfalls: Confusing elementwise multiplication with matrix multiplication
Computing explicit inverses unnecessarily
Interpreting a high-dimensional distance without considering scaling

lessons.title: Represent quantities as vectors
lessons.explain: A vector can represent a direction and magnitude geometrically or a collection of measurements computationally. Coordinates depend on a chosen basis, so the same abstract direction can have different numerical descriptions. A norm measures size; Euclidean distance is the norm of a difference. In a feature vector, however, coordinates may have different units, such as age and income, so raw distance can be dominated by a large numerical scale. Write down what each coordinate means before applying geometric intuition. Draw two-dimensional examples, then extend the same operations to arrays with more coordinates while preserving their interpretation.
lessons.practice: Represent three fictional customers by two features. Compute distances before and after rescaling one feature, draw the points, and explain why nearest-neighbor relationships can change.
lessons.deliverable: A geometric sketch and a scale-sensitivity table.
lessons.check: What is the Euclidean norm of the vector (3, 4)?
lessons.answer: It is sqrt(3 squared + 4 squared)=5. The interpretation assumes the coordinate scaling is meaningful for the chosen geometry.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown vectors essence of linear algebra

lessons.title: Read dot products as alignment
lessons.explain: The dot product combines matching coordinates through multiplication and addition. Geometrically, it relates to vector lengths and the angle between them, so it measures both scale and alignment. A linear prediction is a dot product between feature values and weights plus a bias. Cosine similarity removes magnitude by dividing by both norms, which can be useful when direction matters more than scale, but it is undefined for a zero vector. Projection asks how much of one vector lies along another direction. These ideas later connect ordinary regression, similarity search, attention scores, and interpretation of embedding spaces.
lessons.practice: Compute dot products, cosine similarities, and one-dimensional projections for three two-dimensional vectors. Include perpendicular vectors and a zero-vector edge case with an explicit policy.
lessons.deliverable: A table connecting arithmetic results to geometric sketches.
lessons.check: What is the dot product of (1, 2) and (2, -1), and what does it imply?
lessons.answer: It is 1×2 + 2×(-1)=0. Both vectors are nonzero, so they are orthogonal under the ordinary Euclidean inner product.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown dot products and duality

lessons.title: See matrices as transformations
lessons.explain: A matrix can represent a linear transformation that maps input vectors to output vectors. Its columns show where the input basis vectors go. Matrix multiplication composes transformations, which explains why order usually matters: rotating then stretching is not generally the same as stretching then rotating. In machine learning, a batch matrix can multiply a weight matrix to transform many examples together. Track dimensions as carefully as meanings. If X has shape (samples, input_features) and W has shape (input_features, output_features), the result has shape (samples, output_features). The transpose swaps axes and changes which vectors participate in each dot product.
lessons.practice: Implement a two-dimensional rotation and unequal scaling, apply them in both orders, and compare results. Then multiply a 4-by-3 batch by a 3-by-2 weight matrix and verify one output manually.
lessons.deliverable: Transformation plots and a manually checked batch multiplication.
lessons.check: Can a (4, 3) matrix multiply a (2, 3) matrix directly with matrix multiplication?
lessons.answer: No. The inner dimensions 3 and 2 do not match. Multiplying the first by the transpose of the second would have shapes (4, 3)@(3, 2) and produce (4, 2), if that matches the intended meaning.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown matrix multiplication linear transformations

lessons.title: Solve systems through rank and projection
lessons.explain: A linear system asks for coefficients that combine matrix columns to reproduce a target vector. If the target lies outside their span, no exact solution exists; least squares chooses the combination with the smallest squared residual. At the optimum, that residual is orthogonal to the column space under ordinary unweighted least squares. Rank describes the number of independent directions represented by the columns. Redundant columns can produce multiple coefficient vectors with identical predictions. Distinguish whether you need stable predictions or uniquely interpretable coefficients, and use a numerical least-squares solver rather than assuming every matrix has a safe inverse.
lessons.practice: Solve one exact 2-by-2 system, one overdetermined noisy system, and one system with duplicated columns using numpy.linalg.lstsq. Inspect rank, predictions, and residuals.
lessons.deliverable: Three solved systems with an explanation of uniqueness and residual behavior.
lessons.check: If two feature columns are identical, can their individual regression coefficients always be uniquely identified?
lessons.answer: No. Many coefficient pairs with the same sum produce identical predictions. The design matrix is rank deficient unless additional constraints or regularization determine a particular solution.
lessons.videoQuery: MIT 18.06 least squares projections and rank

lessons.title: Diagnose numerical geometry
lessons.explain: A mathematically solvable system can still be numerically fragile. When columns are nearly dependent, a small change in data may produce a large change in fitted coefficients. Singular values describe how a matrix stretches or compresses different directions; very small values reveal directions with little information. The singular value decomposition also underlies low-rank approximation and later dimensionality reduction. You do not need to implement a production decomposition algorithm now, but you should interpret its outputs. Prefer stable solvers and report sensitivity instead of presenting unstable coefficients as precise discoveries. Geometry explains what the data can and cannot identify.
lessons.practice: Complete the least-squares laboratory. Gradually make two feature columns nearly identical, perturb the target slightly, and compare coefficient changes, prediction changes, and singular values. Document the practical implication.
lessons.deliverable: A sensitivity report and a stable least-squares implementation.
lessons.check: Why can coefficients change dramatically while predictions on the training data barely change?
lessons.answer: Nearly dependent features allow large opposing coefficient changes along weakly identified directions. Those changes cancel in observed predictions, even though the parameter values are unstable.

workedExample.title: A projection splits explained and residual components
workedExample.code:
u = (3.0, 4.0)
v = (1.0, 0.0)
def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
scale = dot(u, v) / dot(v, v)
projection = tuple(scale * x for x in v)
residual = tuple(x - y for x, y in zip(u, projection))
print("projection", projection)
print("residual", residual)
print("residual_dot_v", dot(residual, v))
print("squared_lengths", dot(u, u), dot(projection, projection) + dot(residual, residual))
workedExample.explanation: The projection is the point on the span of v closest to u in Euclidean distance. The residual is perpendicular to that span, which makes its dot product with v zero and gives the squared-length decomposition. Least squares extends this geometry from one direction to the column space of a design matrix. Orthogonality is a property of the fitted projection under its chosen inner product, not proof that the original features are statistically independent or causally meaningful.

assessment.question: In ordinary least squares, a residual orthogonal to the design-matrix column space establishes what?
options: The model is causally correct.
The test error must be zero.
Every input feature is independent of every other feature.
The fitted coefficients minimize the training squared error under the stated linear model.
assessment.explanation: At the least-squares solution, there is no remaining direction inside the model’s column space that can reduce the training squared error by an infinitesimal move. This is an optimization statement. It does not establish causal identification, good extrapolation, absence of leakage or independent features. Generalization and interpretation require additional evidence and assumptions.

connections.before: Array shapes and dot products gain a geometric interpretation.
connections.after: Linear regression, PCA and embedding similarity reuse projection and distance ideas.

modules.title: Probability as reasoning under uncertainty
modules.summary: Model uncertain events, distinguish conditional probabilities, and connect simulation to expected outcomes.
modules.why: Prediction is uncertain because observations are incomplete and the world varies; probability makes those limits explicit.
outcomes: Calculate conditional and joint probabilities
Use Bayes’ rule with base rates
Explain expectation, variance, and sampling variability

project.title: A base-rate and screening simulator
project.brief: Simulate a fictional screening system and compare observed counts with analytical probabilities under different prevalence rates.
deliverables: A probability tree and analytical calculation
A reproducible simulation with several sample sizes
A plain-language interpretation of positive results
A sensitivity analysis over prevalence
rubric: Sensitivity is not confused with positive predictive value
Simulation approaches theoretical proportions with sampling variation
Assumptions about independence and population are explicit

pitfalls: Reversing conditional probabilities
Ignoring base rates
Treating independence as a default fact

lessons.title: Define events and sample spaces
