lessons.explain: Probability assigns weights to possible outcomes under a stated model. A sample space lists the possibilities; an event is a subset of them. The probabilities of mutually exclusive exhaustive outcomes sum to one, but not every event has equal probability. Start by defining the experiment and population clearly, because the same phrase can refer to different events. Complements describe what does not happen, while unions and intersections describe combinations. Counting examples with cards or small tables exposes overlap and double counting. Probability is useful only when the model’s assumptions are connected to the situation you intend to reason about.
lessons.practice: Construct a sample space for two fair coin flips, then for two draws with replacement from a bag with unequal color counts. Calculate complements, unions, and intersections by listing outcomes.
lessons.deliverable: Two outcome tables with probabilities and overlap calculations.
lessons.check: For a fair six-sided die, what is the probability of “even or greater than 4”?
lessons.answer: The event is {2,4,5,6}, so the probability is 4/6=2/3. The overlap {6} must not be counted twice.
lessons.videoQuery: Harvard Stat 110 sample spaces events and probability

lessons.title: Condition on information carefully
lessons.explain: Conditional probability restricts attention to outcomes compatible with known information. P(A given B) asks how often A occurs within the B group, which is generally different from P(B given A). Joint probability concerns both events happening and can be factored using a conditional probability. Independence means learning one event does not change the probability of the other; it is an assumption or property to justify, not a convenient synonym for unrelated-looking variables. A two-way frequency table makes denominators visible and often prevents mistakes more effectively than manipulating formulas without a population picture.
lessons.practice: Build a 100-person fictional table of course attendance and exam success. Compute joint probabilities, both directions of conditional probability, and whether the constructed events are independent.
lessons.deliverable: A two-way table and five probability calculations with denominators labeled.
lessons.check: If 30 of 40 attendees pass and 20 of 60 non-attendees pass, what is P(attendee given pass)?
lessons.answer: There are 50 passes overall, of which 30 are attendees, so the probability is 30/50=0.6. This is different from P(pass given attendee)=30/40=0.75.
lessons.videoQuery: Harvard Stat 110 conditional probability and independence

lessons.title: Update beliefs with Bayes’ rule
lessons.explain: Bayes’ rule relates a probability after observing evidence to the prior prevalence of a hypothesis and the likelihood of that evidence under competing hypotheses. A highly sensitive screening system can still produce mostly false alarms when the condition is rare. The denominator accounts for every way the observed evidence could arise, including false positives. Translate percentages into a hypothetical population of ten thousand people before using a formula; the counts make base rates tangible. The result is conditional on the model and population assumptions, so changing prevalence or measurement quality can change the posterior even when the observed result looks identical.
lessons.practice: For prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, and false-positive rate 5%, calculate expected counts in 10,000 people and the probability of the condition after a positive result. Repeat with prevalence 20%.
lessons.deliverable: Two count diagrams and a comparison of posterior probabilities.
lessons.check: In the 1% prevalence example, what fraction of positive results are true positives?
lessons.answer: There are 90 true positives and 495 false positives, so 90/(90+495) is about 15.4%. High sensitivity alone does not imply a high probability after a positive result.
lessons.videoQuery: 3Blue1Brown Bayes theorem and base rates

lessons.title: Summarize uncertain quantities
lessons.explain: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome, allowing uncertainty to be summarized and calculated. Expectation is a probability-weighted average, not necessarily a value you will observe on one trial. Variance measures the expected squared deviation from that mean, and standard deviation returns the spread to the original units. Different distributions describe different mechanisms: Bernoulli for one binary event, binomial for counts under repeated independent trials, and continuous distributions for measurements. Choose a distribution because its assumptions fit the process, not because its curve is familiar. Pay attention to tails when rare large losses matter more than typical outcomes.
lessons.practice: Calculate expected value and variance for a simple three-outcome payoff. Simulate Bernoulli and binomial outcomes, compare sample summaries with theory, and explain one situation where independence would fail.
lessons.deliverable: Analytical calculations and a simulation comparison.
lessons.check: A fair game pays 0 with probability 0.5 and 10 with probability 0.5. What are its expectation and variance?
lessons.answer: The mean is 5. The variance is 0.5×(0-5) squared + 0.5×(10-5) squared =25; the standard deviation is 5.
lessons.videoQuery: Harvard Stat 110 random variables expectation variance

lessons.title: Use simulation to test probabilistic reasoning
lessons.explain: Simulation generates outcomes from an assumed model so you can inspect its consequences. It is especially useful for checking a probability calculation or exploring a process that is awkward to solve exactly. A random seed helps reproduce a particular run, but it does not remove uncertainty or prove the assumptions are realistic. As the number of independent samples grows, averages tend to stabilize under suitable conditions; they do not become exact after an arbitrary threshold. Compare several seeds and sample sizes, and distinguish Monte Carlo noise from model error. A precisely simulated unrealistic model remains an unrealistic description of the world.
lessons.practice: Complete the screening simulator for several prevalence rates and sample sizes. Compare simulated positive predictive values to analytical results, repeat with multiple seeds, and explain the variability when positives are rare.
lessons.deliverable: A reproducible simulation report with analytical cross-checks.
lessons.check: Does using the same random seed for every experiment prove a result is robust?
lessons.answer: No. It makes one random sequence repeatable. Robustness requires checking relevant variation, including other seeds, samples, assumptions, and populations.

workedExample.title: Count base rates before interpreting a flag
workedExample.code:
population = 10_000
prevalence = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.90
false_positive_rate = 0.05
true_flags = population * prevalence * sensitivity
false_flags = population * (1 - prevalence) * false_positive_rate
posterior = true_flags / (true_flags + false_flags)
print("true_flags", round(true_flags))
print("false_flags", round(false_flags))
print(f"P(event | flag) = {posterior:.2%}")
workedExample.explanation: Among 10,000 expected observations, 100 contain the event and the detector flags 90 of them. Of the 9,900 non-events, it flags 495 incorrectly. A positive flag therefore means something very different from a 90% probability of an event. The sensitivity conditions on an event already being present; the posterior conditions on seeing a flag. These are different populations. This arithmetic assumes the stated rates remain applicable to the deployment population, which is itself a claim to investigate.

assessment.question: A detector’s sensitivity is 90%. Does a positive result imply a 90% probability that the event is present?
options: No; the posterior also depends on prevalence and false-positive rate.
Yes; sensitivity and the probability after a positive result are identical.
No; a positive result always has probability 50%.
Yes, provided the detector is implemented in Python.
assessment.explanation: Sensitivity is P(flag given event). The question after observing a flag is P(event given flag). Bayes’ rule connects them through the event’s base rate and the rate of false flags. When the event is rare, even a modest false-positive rate can dominate the pool of positive results. Deployment base rates matter even if sensitivity remains unchanged.

connections.before: Algebraic ratios become statements about explicitly conditioned populations.
connections.after: Calibration, decision thresholds and uncertainty estimates depend on distinguishing these probabilities.

modules.title: Statistics, experiments, and causal restraint
modules.summary: Learn what a sample can support, quantify uncertainty, and design comparisons that answer a clear question.
modules.why: Model evaluation and product experiments are statistical arguments; confidence comes from design and assumptions as much as from formulas.
outcomes: Distinguish estimands, estimates, and uncertainty
Interpret confidence intervals and p-values correctly
Design a basic randomized comparison and recognize confounding

project.title: An honest experiment analysis
project.brief: Analyze a simulated randomized onboarding experiment with a prespecified outcome, uncertainty interval, and practical decision rule.
deliverables: Experiment plan with unit of randomization and primary metric
Effect estimate with uncertainty and assumption checks
A report distinguishing statistical and practical significance
A sensitivity note on missing outcomes and subgroup exploration
rubric: No causal claim is made from an uncontrolled correlation
The interval is interpreted using its actual frequentist meaning
Exploratory analyses are labeled and not sold as confirmatory

pitfalls: Interpreting a p-value as the probability the null is true
Repeatedly peeking until a desired threshold is crossed
Ignoring selection bias or dependent observations

lessons.title: Separate population questions from sample answers
lessons.explain: A statistical question needs a target population and a quantity of interest, called an estimand. A sample provides an estimate of that quantity, but its usefulness depends on how observations entered the dataset. A large convenience sample can remain biased if the selection process excludes important groups. Measurement can also differ from the concept you care about: clicks are not necessarily satisfaction, and recorded activity is not necessarily learning. Write down who is represented, who is missing, and the unit of observation. This framing comes before choosing a formula because no statistical package can infer the population you intended to describe.
lessons.practice: Compare a survey of all registered learners with a survey answered only by course completers. Define three estimands, identify selection mechanisms, and construct a small example where the completer average is misleading.
lessons.deliverable: A population/sample diagram and a bias analysis.
lessons.check: Why does increasing a biased sample from 1,000 to 1,000,000 observations not necessarily remove the bias?
lessons.answer: More observations reduce random sampling variability under the same process, but they do not correct systematic exclusion or measurement errors built into that process.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistics sampling selection bias and estimands

lessons.title: Estimate uncertainty with repeated-sample logic
lessons.explain: An estimate varies across samples even when the underlying population is fixed. Its sampling distribution describes that variation, and the standard error summarizes the spread of the estimator rather than the spread of individual observations. A frequentist confidence procedure is designed to cover the fixed target in a stated proportion of repeated samples under its assumptions. Bootstrap resampling approximates sampling variation by resampling observed units with replacement, but the units must reflect dependence and the original sample must be informative. Neither a narrow interval nor many bootstrap repetitions repairs selection bias. Interpret uncertainty as conditional on the design and assumptions that produced it.
lessons.practice: Generate repeated samples from a known distribution, calculate sample means and intervals, and measure empirical coverage. Then bootstrap a small dataset and compare the interval with the repeated-sampling experiment.
lessons.deliverable: A coverage simulation and a plain-language interval interpretation.
lessons.check: Does a realized 95% frequentist confidence interval mean there is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies inside it?
lessons.answer: Not under the standard frequentist interpretation. The procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions; the particular realized interval either covers it or does not.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistics confidence intervals bootstrap sampling distributions

lessons.title: Test hypotheses without threshold worship
lessons.explain: A hypothesis test compares observed data with what a specified null model would predict. A p-value is the probability, under that null and the test assumptions, of a result at least as extreme according to the chosen statistic. It is not the probability that the null is true or that the result happened by chance. Effect size and uncertainty explain practical importance more directly than a threshold alone. Testing many hypotheses or repeatedly inspecting accumulating data changes false-positive behavior unless the design accounts for it. Prespecify the main question and distinguish planned analysis from exploration so readers can assess the evidence fairly.
lessons.practice: Simulate 100 independent tests under a null model and count small p-values. Compare a tiny effect in a huge sample with a larger effect in a small sample, reporting both effect size and uncertainty.
lessons.deliverable: A multiple-testing demonstration and two balanced result summaries.
lessons.check: If 100 independent true null hypotheses are tested at a 0.05 threshold without correction, how many false positives are expected?
lessons.answer: Five on average, because the expected count is 100×0.05. The actual count varies, and the probability of at least one is much larger than 0.05.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistics p values effect sizes and multiple testing

lessons.title: Distinguish prediction from intervention
lessons.explain: Prediction asks what is likely to happen given observed information; causal inference asks what would change under an intervention. A variable can predict an outcome without causing it, especially when a common cause influences both. Random assignment helps balance measured and unmeasured factors in expectation, making a comparison more interpretable when implementation and follow-up are sound. Define the treatment, comparison, outcome, unit of randomization, and analysis population before collecting data. Consider spillovers and repeated observations: randomizing individuals may be inappropriate when people influence one another. A causal claim is a claim about a design and assumptions, not just a correlation coefficient.
lessons.practice: Draw a causal diagram for study time, prior preparation, and exam score. Design a randomized reminder experiment and specify the primary outcome, assignment unit, eligibility rules, and one possible interference problem.
lessons.deliverable: A causal diagram and a one-page experiment protocol.
lessons.check: Why does a correlation between taking an advanced course and higher salary not establish the course caused the salary difference?
lessons.answer: Prior skill, motivation, experience, location, and selection into the course may affect both enrollment and salary. A credible causal design must address these alternative explanations.
lessons.videoQuery: Causal inference randomized experiments confounding introduction

lessons.title: Write an experiment report that survives scrutiny
lessons.explain: An experiment report should let a reader reconstruct the question, design, analysis, and decision. Start with the prespecified primary outcome and show the effect estimate with an uncertainty interval before discussing secondary patterns. Report missing outcomes, exclusions, assignment problems, and any deviations from the plan. A statistically detectable improvement may be too small to justify cost, while an inconclusive result may still rule out a large benefit. Use a practical decision rule tied to consequences rather than treating a conventional p-value threshold as a product strategy. Label exploratory subgroup findings as hypotheses for further work rather than confirmed discoveries.
lessons.practice: Complete the simulated onboarding experiment. Estimate the treatment effect, compute an interval, evaluate a minimum worthwhile improvement, and examine how missing outcomes could change the conclusion.
lessons.deliverable: An experiment report with a clear decision and explicit limitations.
lessons.check: An estimated improvement is 0.2 percentage points with a narrow interval above zero, but deployment requires at least 2 points to justify its cost. What follows?
lessons.answer: The result may be statistically distinguishable from zero yet practically insufficient. The deployment decision should reflect the prespecified minimum worthwhile benefit and relevant costs.

workedExample.title: An exact randomization test can have limited resolution
workedExample.code:
from itertools import combinations
outcomes = [9, 8, 7, 3, 2, 1]
def difference(treated):
    control = set(range(6)) - set(treated)
    return sum(outcomes[i] for i in treated) / 3 - sum(outcomes[i] for i in control) / 3
observed = difference((0, 1, 2))
null_differences = [difference(group) for group in combinations(range(6), 3)]
p_value = sum(abs(d) >= abs(observed) for d in null_differences) / len(null_differences)
print("observed_difference", observed)
print("possible_assignments", len(null_differences))
print("two_sided_p", p_value)
workedExample.explanation: Suppose exactly three of six units were assigned treatment uniformly at random. Under a sharp null of no treatment effect, the six outcomes can be held fixed while enumerating all 20 possible assignments. The observed separation looks large, but two assignments are at least this extreme in absolute value, yielding 0.1. A tiny study has limited inferential resolution. The test’s validity depends on the actual assignment mechanism; applying the same permutation to observational groups does not erase confounding.

assessment.question: This randomization test returns p = 0.1. Which interpretation is valid?
options: There is a 10% probability that the null is true.
Under the stated null and randomization mechanism, 10% of assignments are at least as extreme by this statistic.
There is a 90% probability the treatment works for everyone.
The estimated effect is exactly zero.
assessment.explanation: A p-value is a probability of data or a statistic under a specified model and procedure. It is not the posterior probability of that model and does not describe the chance that the treatment benefits an individual. This example also shows why effect size, uncertainty, study design and decision consequences should be reported alongside a thresholded significance judgment.

connections.before: Conditional probability now supports statements about a procedure’s sampling behavior.
connections.after: Model comparison and product experiments need the same restraint about what an observed difference establishes.

modules.title: Explore data without fooling yourself
modules.summary: Use tables and visualizations to understand distributions, quality, relationships, and the limits of an analysis.
modules.why: Exploration discovers problems and hypotheses; disciplined reporting prevents attractive charts from becoming unsupported conclusions.
outcomes: Profile data quality and distributions
Choose charts that answer a specific question
Document findings separately from hypotheses and limitations

project.title: A reproducible data investigation
project.brief: Analyze a public or synthetic tabular dataset with a documented question, quality audit, targeted charts, and a restrained conclusion.
deliverables: Data provenance and dictionary
A reproducible analysis script or notebook
Six purposeful charts with captions
A findings ledger separating observations from hypotheses
rubric: Plots identify units, population, and denominators
Missingness and exclusions are reported
No evaluation target information is used to fit future preprocessing

pitfalls: Choosing plots because they look impressive
Treating missingness as random without checking
Exploring the held-out test set until it becomes training feedback

lessons.title: Start with provenance and data quality
lessons.explain: Before asking what a dataset reveals, ask how it came to exist. Identify its source, collection process, unit of observation, permissions, and relevant time period. Profile schema, missing values, duplicate keys, impossible ranges, and suspicious category variants. An outlier may be an error, a rare valid case, or the most important event in the dataset; automatic removal can erase the phenomenon you need to understand. Preserve raw data and record every transformation. A quality audit is not an attempt to make all columns look tidy, but an investigation into which questions the available evidence can responsibly answer.
lessons.practice: Audit a small dataset with intentional duplicate identifiers, mixed date formats, missing categories, and an extreme but valid value. Classify each issue and propose a documented handling policy.
lessons.deliverable: A quality report with counts, examples, and treatment decisions.
lessons.check: Why is removing every value more than three standard deviations from the mean not a universal cleaning rule?
lessons.answer: Distributions may be skewed or heavy-tailed, and extreme values may be valid or central to the task. Removal requires domain and measurement evidence, not only a generic distance threshold.
lessons.videoQuery: Pandas getting started missing data and data cleaning

lessons.title: Read distributions before averages
lessons.explain: A single average can hide multiple populations, skew, or rare extreme values. Histograms show how observations occupy ranges, but bin choices affect the apparent shape. Quantiles describe positions in the distribution, while median and interquartile range are less sensitive to extreme values than mean and standard deviation. Use several summaries that answer the actual question: a service’s median latency describes a typical request, while a high percentile exposes a slower tail experienced by some users. Inspect sample size and missingness alongside every summary. A distribution is evidence about the observed population and measurement process, not automatically a universal law.
lessons.practice: Compare a symmetric distribution, a skewed distribution, and a mixture with the same approximate mean. Plot histograms with several bin widths and report median, quartiles, mean, and a high percentile.
lessons.deliverable: Three distribution profiles with captions explaining what the mean misses.
lessons.check: Why might median response time stay stable while users complain about worsening service?
lessons.answer: The slow tail may worsen for a minority of requests while the middle remains unchanged. High-percentile latency and segment-level analysis can reveal that experience.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistics histograms quantiles skew and robust summaries

lessons.title: Plot relationships and expose confounders
lessons.explain: A relationship between two variables can change when observations are separated into meaningful groups. Scatterplots reveal shape, spread, and unusual cases that a single correlation number can miss. Stratifying by time, cohort, or a plausible confounder can expose whether an aggregate pattern is mixing different processes. Simpson’s paradox occurs when an association reverses after grouping because the composition of the groups matters. This does not mean every aggregate analysis is wrong; it means the question and causal structure determine which comparison is relevant. Use exploratory patterns to formulate hypotheses and investigate data collection, not to declare causation from a visually persuasive trend.
lessons.practice: Construct or find a small two-group example where an aggregate trend differs from within-group trends. Plot both views, compute group sizes, and explain the role of composition.
lessons.deliverable: An aggregate plot, stratified plots, and an interpretation note.
lessons.check: Can two variables have zero linear correlation while still being strongly related?
lessons.answer: Yes. For a symmetric X and Y=X squared, the linear correlation can be zero even though Y is completely determined by X. A scatterplot reveals the nonlinear relationship.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistics correlation Simpson paradox and scatterplots

lessons.title: Design charts for honest comparison
lessons.explain: A chart is an argument made through position, length, color, and labeling. Choose an encoding that matches the comparison: position is usually effective for quantitative differences, while color can distinguish categories when contrast and labels remain accessible. State units, population, time period, and denominators. Bar lengths normally require a meaningful zero baseline; line charts may use a focused range when the scale is clearly labeled and the question justifies it. Avoid decorative depth, unexplained dual axes, and color-only distinctions. A useful caption states the observable pattern and its main limitation so readers do not have to infer the claim from the title.
lessons.practice: Redesign three misleading charts: a truncated bar chart, counts compared across unequal populations, and a red/green-only category plot. Add accessible labels and captions.
lessons.deliverable: Before/after charts with an explanation of each correction.
lessons.check: Why can comparing raw complaint counts across two products with very different user bases mislead?
lessons.answer: Counts mix exposure with complaint propensity. A relevant rate such as complaints per active user, with consistent definitions and uncertainty, supports a fairer comparison.
lessons.videoQuery: Data visualization principles chart scales and accessibility

lessons.title: Turn exploration into a reproducible evidence brief
lessons.explain: Exploration is iterative, but the final analysis should run in a clear order from raw data to conclusions. Hidden notebook state can make a result depend on cells executed hours earlier, so restart and run the complete workflow before sharing. Separate directly observed facts from interpretations and hypotheses. For each finding, identify the supporting table or chart, the population covered, and a limitation that could change the conclusion. Keep a record of exclusions and transformations. A strong brief can say that the available data do not answer a tempting question; that restraint protects the next modeling or product decision from false confidence.
lessons.practice: Complete the data investigation with six purposeful charts and a findings ledger. Run everything from a clean session, verify reported numbers, and identify two questions requiring new data or an experiment.
lessons.deliverable: A reproducible analysis and a concise evidence brief.
lessons.check: What distinguishes an observation from a hypothesis in an exploration report?
lessons.answer: An observation describes a result directly supported by the analyzed data and definitions. A hypothesis proposes an explanation or broader relationship that needs additional evidence or a suitable design.

workedExample.title: Averages can hide two different data stories
workedExample.code:
from statistics import mean, median
sales = [10, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 100]
print("n", len(sales))
print(f"mean {mean(sales):.2f}")
print("median", median(sales))
print("minimum", min(sales))
print("maximum", max(sales))
print("largest_share", round(max(sales) / sum(sales), 3))
workedExample.expected:
n 7
mean 23.71
median 11
minimum 10
maximum 100
largest_share 0.602
workedExample.explanation: The mean answers a total-per-observation question and is pulled upward by the large value. The median describes the middle observation and changes much less. Neither statistic tells you whether 100 is a valid large sale, a unit error or a duplicate. That requires provenance and a domain check. Plot or inspect the distribution, retain the original observations, and label any cleaning decision. Removing the value solely because it makes a chart awkward would replace investigation with a preferred story.

assessment.question: An unusually large value raises the mean substantially. What should happen first?
options: Delete it because means should be close to medians.
Replace every value with the mean.
Investigate its provenance, units and validity before choosing a treatment.
Assume it proves a new causal mechanism.
assessment.explanation: An extreme value can be an error, a real rare event, or evidence that the data mix different processes. The appropriate action depends on the question and provenance. Describe its influence, check the raw record and units, and document a defensible policy. Robust summaries can help, but they do not decide whether a particular observation is valid.

connections.before: Statistical summaries acquire meaning through the dataset’s grain and measurement process.
connections.after: The data audit constrains the target, features, split and baseline in c12.

modules.why: The validity of a model result depends on target construction, data availability, and evaluation design before any algorithm is trained.
outcomes: Define features, targets, prediction time, and decision policy
Choose random, grouped, or temporal splits deliberately
Compare simple baselines on an untouched final evaluation set

project.brief: Specify and implement the evaluation design for a fictional subscription-renewal predictor, including a non-ML baseline.
deliverables: Prediction charter with decision time and available information
Target-construction and split code
A majority/rule baseline with appropriate metrics
A leakage audit and a sealed test-set policy

Model selection is separated from final evaluation

pitfalls: Randomly splitting dependent or temporal observations
Fitting preprocessing on all data before splitting
Using the test set repeatedly to choose features or thresholds

lessons.title: Turn a decision into a learning contract
lessons.explain: Supervised learning uses examples of inputs and desired outputs to estimate a mapping that may generalize to new cases. The target must correspond to a well-defined event, and features must be available when the prediction is made. The prediction itself is not the final decision: a probability may feed a threshold, ranking, or human workflow with its own costs. Define the population, prediction time, outcome window, label availability, and intended intervention. Ask whether the target is measurable and whether a prediction can actually improve the decision. A precise learning contract prevents the model from solving an easier historical question that cannot exist in production.
lessons.practice: Write a charter for predicting subscription renewal seven days before expiry. Define the observation window, outcome window, available fields, decision recipient, and how delayed or ambiguous labels are handled.
lessons.deliverable: A one-page learning contract with a timeline diagram.
lessons.check: Why is “predict whether a customer renews” incomplete as a task definition?
lessons.answer: It omits when the prediction occurs, which customers are eligible, what counts as renewal, the outcome horizon, available information, and how the prediction changes a decision.
lessons.videoQuery: Google machine learning problem framing supervised learning

lessons.title: Choose splits that resemble deployment
lessons.explain: A split estimates performance on the kind of unseen data represented by the held-out portion. Random row splitting assumes rows are suitably exchangeable, which fails when records from the same person, device, or time sequence share information. Group splitting keeps related entities together; temporal splitting respects the direction of time. Training data fit model parameters, validation data guide choices, and a final test set estimates the chosen procedure after those choices are settled. No split guarantees future performance under arbitrary change, so explain which deployment scenario it approximates and what shifts remain untested.
lessons.practice: Create a dataset with repeated customer records across months. Compare random, customer-grouped, and temporal splits, checking entity overlap and timestamp order. Choose a split aligned with one explicit deployment scenario.
lessons.deliverable: Three split audits and a justified final design.
lessons.check: Why can a random row split overestimate performance when each patient has multiple nearly identical measurements?
lessons.answer: Measurements from the same patient can appear in both training and evaluation, allowing the model to exploit patient-specific patterns rather than generalize to unseen patients.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit learn cross validation grouped and time series splits

lessons.title: Find leakage in features and transformations
lessons.explain: Leakage occurs when training or evaluation uses information that would not legitimately be available in the intended prediction setting. A cancellation reason recorded after cancellation is an obvious target proxy; a normalization statistic fitted using held-out data is a subtler contamination. Leakage can enter through joins, duplicate records, manual feature selection, or repeated evaluation feedback. For every feature, ask when and how it is generated and whether the real system can know it at prediction time. Fit learned preprocessing only on the training portion within each evaluation fold. A high score is a reason to inspect the pipeline carefully, not a reason to relax scrutiny.
lessons.practice: Audit ten candidate renewal features, including refund amount, later support notes, last-month usage, and customer ID. Mark availability and leakage risk, then demonstrate how preprocessing must be fit on training data only.
lessons.deliverable: A feature availability ledger and a corrected preprocessing example.
lessons.check: Why is filling missing values with a median computed from the entire dataset a form of evaluation contamination?
lessons.answer: The transformation has learned distribution information from held-out observations. Fit the median on training data, then apply that fixed value to validation and test data.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit learn common pitfalls data leakage pipelines

lessons.title: Establish baselines and choose useful metrics
lessons.explain: A model needs a baseline that represents what happens without sophisticated learning. For classification, always predicting the common class can reveal how misleading accuracy is under imbalance; a simple rule may better represent the current workflow. Choose metrics that reflect the decision and its error costs, and report the underlying confusion counts so ratios remain interpretable. A ranking task may prioritize the cases a team can inspect, while a probability forecast needs probability quality. Keep a naive baseline and a practical baseline when they answer different questions. Improvement must be measured under the same data definition and split so the comparison is fair.
lessons.practice: Evaluate an always-renew baseline and one simple usage rule on an imbalanced synthetic renewal dataset. Report confusion counts, precision, recall, and accuracy, then connect false positives and false negatives to the intended action.
lessons.deliverable: A baseline report with metric definitions and an error-cost discussion.
lessons.check: If 95% of customers renew, what accuracy does an always-renew classifier achieve, and what does it reveal about non-renewers?
lessons.answer: It achieves 95% accuracy but identifies none of the non-renewers. A high overall accuracy can coexist with complete failure on the class relevant to retention action.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit learn dummy estimators classification metrics

lessons.title: Seal the evaluation design before tuning
lessons.explain: An evaluation protocol is a commitment about how evidence will be generated. Save split membership, target definitions, preprocessing rules, metrics, and the model-selection procedure before comparing many models. Use validation or cross-validation for iteration and reserve the final test set for a limited, clearly reported assessment. Once its results influence your choices, it no longer functions as untouched evidence for those choices. Keep an experiment log that records both successful and failed attempts, including seeds and data versions. The goal is not ceremonial purity; it is to prevent repeated feedback from turning an apparently objective score into a hidden training signal.
lessons.practice: Complete the prediction charter, split code, leakage ledger, and baseline report. Write a protocol describing model-selection use of validation data and the conditions for opening the final test set.
lessons.deliverable: A runnable evaluation scaffold and a signed-off protocol checklist.
lessons.check: After seeing weak test performance, you change the feature set and report a better score on the same test data. What changed about the evidence?
lessons.answer: The test set has influenced model selection and is no longer untouched evidence for the revised procedure. Report that reuse honestly and seek a fresh holdout or a properly nested evaluation design.

workedExample.title: A split must match the population claim
workedExample.code:
records = [("A", 1), ("A", 2), ("B", 1), ("B", 2)]
row_train, row_test = records[::2], records[1::2]
group_train = [r for r in records if r[0] == "A"]
group_test = [r for r in records if r[0] == "B"]
def overlap(train, test):
    return {person for person, _ in train} & {person for person, _ in test}
print("row_split_overlap", sorted(overlap(row_train, row_test)))
print("group_split_overlap", sorted(overlap(group_train, group_test)))
workedExample.explanation: The row split asks about later records from people already represented in training. The group split asks about a different person. Neither automatically answers every deployment question, and the sample is too small for a useful performance estimate. The point is to expose the claim encoded by the split. Features must also be available at prediction time: separating people does not fix a feature derived from future outcomes. Write down the intended population and cutoff before creating the holdout.

assessment.question: You want to predict outcomes for entirely new hospitals, but random patient rows from every hospital appear in training and test. What is the main problem?
options: Random splitting is always invalid for every dataset.
Every hospital must have exactly the same number of patients.
A larger neural network automatically fixes the evaluation target.
The test may measure transfer within known hospitals rather than to unseen hospitals.
assessment.explanation: The evaluation population differs from the claimed deployment population. Shared hospital-specific patterns can make a random row split optimistic for transfer to a new hospital. Holding out entire hospitals is more aligned with that claim, while still requiring enough groups, uncertainty reporting and checks for other leakage. Split design follows the question, not a universal preference for one method.

connections.before: Exploratory findings and domain assumptions become an explicit evaluation protocol.
connections.after: Every model comparison that follows must preserve this protocol and its information boundaries.

modules.title: Linear models: learn an objective, not a formula
modules.summary: Build regression and classification from assumptions, losses, and held-out evidence.
modules.why: Simple models expose the link between representation, optimization, and generalization before complex models obscure it.
outcomes: Derive squared-error and logistic objectives
Fit regularized baselines without contaminating evaluation
Explain coefficients and their limitations

project.title: A trustworthy linear baseline
project.brief: Predict a numeric target and a binary outcome using separate, documented baselines on a small tabular dataset.
deliverables: Dataset card and split rationale
NumPy gradient implementation checked against a library
Regularization comparison and error analysis
rubric: Training transformations are fitted only on training rows
Gradient checks agree within a stated tolerance
Conclusions use held-out metrics and compare a dummy baseline

pitfalls: Interpreting correlation as causation
Scaling before the split
Treating accuracy as the objective for every classifier

lessons.title: From prediction to squared error
lessons.explain: A linear predictor assigns one weight to each feature and adds an intercept. This is a restriction on the function you can learn, not a claim that the world is linear. Squared error penalizes large residuals strongly; minimizing its average chooses the best fit under that penalty. Compare the model with predicting the training mean: without that comparison, a small-looking error has no interpretation. Units matter because squared errors have squared target units. Plot residuals against predictions and meaningful features to detect systematic structure, unequal variance, and cases the model fails to represent.
lessons.practice: Generate y = 3x + 2 plus noise; compare a training-mean baseline, least squares, and a deliberately misspecified straight line on quadratic data.
lessons.deliverable: A plot of fitted lines and held-out RMSE for three settings.
lessons.check: If every target is multiplied by ten, how do MSE and RMSE change for equally rescaled predictions?
lessons.answer: Residuals multiply by ten. MSE multiplies by one hundred, while RMSE multiplies by ten; RMSE retains target units.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR linear regression loss and residual analysis

lessons.title: Gradients as local instructions
lessons.explain: The gradient describes how a differentiable loss changes under a small parameter movement. Moving against it can reduce loss locally; it does not guarantee a useful result for an arbitrary step size. For squared-error regression, differentiating the prediction and residual gives a vectorized gradient. Check each coordinate against a central finite difference before trusting an optimizer. Feature scales affect the shape of the loss surface: one direction can be much steeper than another, causing unstable steps. Standardization often improves conditioning, but its mean and scale must be estimated from training data alone.
lessons.practice: Implement batch gradient descent for a two-feature regression, verify gradients numerically, and plot loss with three learning rates before and after standardization.
lessons.deliverable: A reusable fit function plus gradient-check and convergence figures.
lessons.check: What does a loss that alternates between increasingly large values suggest?
lessons.answer: The step size may be too large relative to curvature; inspect gradients and data scaling, then reduce the learning rate. Also check the loss and gradient implementation.
lessons.videoQuery: Stanford CS229 linear regression gradient descent

lessons.title: Probabilities through logistic regression
lessons.explain: A linear score can be transformed into a number between zero and one with the sigmoid function. Logistic regression models log odds as a linear function of features. Bernoulli negative log likelihood becomes binary cross entropy: confident wrong predictions incur a large cost. A probability estimate is separate from a decision, which also requires a threshold and consequences for errors. A threshold of one half is a convention under particular costs, not a universal law. Use stable library loss implementations because taking logarithms of rounded probabilities can produce infinities and hide numerical mistakes.
lessons.practice: Fit logistic regression to an imbalanced binary dataset; compute log loss and a confusion matrix at thresholds 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8.
lessons.deliverable: A threshold table explaining false-positive and false-negative tradeoffs.
lessons.check: Can two classifiers have identical accuracy but different log loss?
lessons.answer: Yes. They can make the same thresholded decisions while assigning different probabilities. Log loss also evaluates confidence, so a confidently wrong model can score much worse.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR logistic regression and classification thresholds

lessons.title: Regularization is an explicit preference
lessons.explain: Many parameter settings can fit limited observations, especially with correlated or numerous features. Regularization adds a preference for simpler parameter values to the empirical loss. L2 shrinkage discourages large squared weights; L1 can set some weights exactly to zero. Both alter the fitted model and can improve prediction at the cost of additional bias. Penalty strength depends on feature scaling and library conventions, so compare validation behavior rather than transferring numbers blindly. Keep the test set outside this selection process. Correlated features also make individual coefficients unstable even when predictions remain fairly stable.
lessons.practice: Compare unregularized, ridge, and lasso models on synthetic correlated features; use a training-only scaling pipeline and cross-validation to select strength.
lessons.deliverable: Coefficient paths and a validation curve with a selected penalty.
lessons.check: Does a zero lasso coefficient prove that a feature has no causal effect?
lessons.answer: No. Selection depends on the data, correlated alternatives, scaling, penalty, and objective. Predictive exclusion neither establishes nor rules out causation.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR ridge regression lasso regularization

lessons.title: Write a baseline that can be challenged
lessons.explain: A useful baseline is a reproducible argument, not merely a score. Record what the model sees, when information becomes available, which examples belong in each split, and the metric that represents the decision. Compare a dummy predictor, a linear predictor, and one justified feature transformation. Inspect individual errors and slices that matter operationally, without using the final test set for repeated redesign. Report what would invalidate the conclusion, such as a new population or a change in label collection. This creates a reference against which later complexity must earn its maintenance cost.
lessons.practice: Package the module project as one command that trains on a fixed split, saves predictions, and emits a short model report including three manually reviewed errors.
lessons.deliverable: A reproducible baseline report and prediction artifact.
lessons.check: A nonlinear model improves validation RMSE by 0.2% but doubles latency. What additional evidence is needed before adopting it?
lessons.answer: Estimate whether the gain is robust across suitable resamples and valuable in the application, then compare latency, cost, failure slices, and maintenance burden. A tiny point improvement alone is insufficient.
lessons.videoQuery: Google machine learning crash course production ML baselines

workedExample.title: One gradient update is a calculation you can audit
workedExample.code:
x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
y = [2.0, 4.0, 6.0]
w = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
for step in range(2):
    errors = [w * a - b for a, b in zip(x, y)]
    loss = sum(e * e for e in errors) / len(x)
    gradient = 2 * sum(e * a for e, a in zip(errors, x)) / len(x)
    print(f"step={step} w={w:.4f} loss={loss:.4f} gradient={gradient:.4f}")
    w -= learning_rate * gradient
workedExample.expected:
step=0 w=0.0000 loss=18.6667 gradient=-18.6667
step=1 w=1.8667 loss=0.0830 gradient=-1.2444
workedExample.explanation: The prediction is wx, so the chain rule multiplies each residual’s squared-loss derivative by its input x. Averaging gives the gradient of the mean squared error. The negative gradient at w=0 directs an increase in w, and a modest update reduces the training loss. The toy relationship is noiseless and has no intercept; it illustrates optimization rather than realistic predictive performance. A successful loss decrease does not establish that the train/test split is valid or that the model will extrapolate.

assessment.question: Training loss falls after every update. What can you conclude?
options: The update procedure is improving this training objective, but generalization needs separate evidence.
The model cannot be overfitting.
The coefficients must represent causal effects.
The test set can now be used repeatedly for feature selection.
assessment.explanation: Optimization and generalization answer different questions. Training loss measures fit to the data and objective the optimizer sees. It can decrease while holdout performance worsens, a leaked feature dominates, or the model becomes poorly calibrated. Keep the evaluation protocol intact and compare simple baselines before interpreting a low training loss as a useful system.

connections.before: Projection geometry and derivatives explain the objective and its update direction.
connections.after: Regularization, nonlinear models and neural networks extend this same objective–optimization–evaluation separation.

Compare bagging with boosting
Tune complexity within a valid evaluation design

project.title: Tabular model tournament
project.brief: Compare a linear baseline, constrained tree, random forest, and gradient boosting model using one fixed evaluation protocol.
deliverables: Shared preprocessing and split specification
Runtime and validation comparison
Interpretability caveat and final model recommendation

Hyperparameters are chosen without final-test feedback
Recommendation considers error, cost, and stability

pitfalls: Unlimited trees memorizing noise
Mistaking feature importance for causality
Unfair tuning budgets between models

lessons.title: A tree asks a sequence of questions
lessons.explain: A decision tree partitions feature space by asking questions such as whether a value is below a threshold. Each terminal region makes a constant prediction: often a mean for regression or class proportions for classification. Training greedily chooses splits that improve an impurity criterion on the current data. Greedy improvement is not a guarantee of a globally optimal tree. Deep trees can isolate individual observations and fit noise, so constrain depth, leaf size, or pruning. Small data changes can produce different early splits, which explains both the appeal of trees and their instability.
lessons.practice: Fit trees of depth 1, 3, and unlimited depth to a noisy two-dimensional dataset; draw decision regions and compare training with validation errors.
lessons.deliverable: Decision-boundary figures and a depth-versus-error chart.
lessons.check: Why can an unrestricted regression tree achieve almost zero training error yet generalize poorly?
lessons.answer: It can create leaves containing single observations and memorize their noise. Those tiny regions have high variance and do not reliably describe new observations.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR decision trees regression and classification

lessons.title: Bagging reduces unstable variation
lessons.explain: Bagging trains unstable learners on bootstrap samples and averages their predictions. Averaging helps most when individual errors are not perfectly correlated. Random forests add feature randomness at each split to reduce correlation between trees. More trees usually stabilize the ensemble but do not automatically fix biased data or leakage. Out-of-bag predictions use trees that did not train on a particular observation, providing a convenient estimate under the sampling assumptions. They are not a replacement for a time-based or grouped split when deployment requires one. Computational cost grows with trees, data, and split searches.
lessons.practice: Train forests with increasing tree counts and feature subsampling; compare out-of-bag and held-out scores while recording runtime.
lessons.deliverable: A convergence plot showing metric stability and compute cost.
lessons.check: Would averaging one hundred identical trees reduce their prediction error?
lessons.answer: No. Identical predictions have perfectly correlated errors, so their average is unchanged. Diversity is essential to the variance-reduction benefit.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR bagging random forests and out-of-bag error

lessons.title: Boosting corrects the current model
lessons.explain: Boosting builds an additive predictor sequentially. Each new learner is chosen to improve the current ensemble under a loss; for squared error this resembles fitting residuals. A learning rate shrinks each contribution, trading slower learning for additional control. Tree depth, iteration count, shrinkage, and regularization interact, so increasing one parameter in isolation can mislead. Validation-based early stopping chooses when further optimization stops helping on unseen examples. That stopping set has influenced training decisions and should not be presented as an untouched test set. Boosting is powerful on tabular data but remains vulnerable to unsuitable splits.
lessons.practice: Fit gradient boosting with two learning rates and staged validation tracking; identify the selected iteration and compare with a forest.
lessons.deliverable: Learning curves and a written explanation of the chosen stopping point.
lessons.check: Why is the early-stopping validation score an optimistic final estimate if many settings were compared on it?
lessons.answer: The validation data influenced model selection repeatedly. Selection can exploit random favorable fluctuations, so a separate final test or suitable nested evaluation is needed.
lessons.videoQuery: ISLR boosting additive models and shrinkage

lessons.title: Interpret predictions without inventing causes
lessons.explain: An explanation method answers a particular question about a fitted predictor, not necessarily about the world. Permutation importance asks how predictive performance changes when a feature is shuffled, potentially creating unrealistic combinations when features are correlated. Partial dependence averages predictions after modifying one feature, which can also move outside observed support. Built-in impurity importance can favor features with many split opportunities. Compare methods with domain knowledge and direct error inspection. State which data distribution and model each explanation concerns; none of these techniques alone turns an observational predictive relationship into a causal conclusion.
lessons.practice: Calculate impurity and validation permutation importance on a dataset with correlated and high-cardinality noise features; compare their rankings.
lessons.deliverable: An explanation report identifying one misleading importance result.
lessons.check: Two interchangeable features each receive low permutation importance. Does that imply neither matters?
lessons.answer: No. The unshuffled feature may substitute for the shuffled one. Correlation and redundancy can distribute or hide predictive importance; joint perturbation or redesigned analysis may be more informative.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn permutation feature importance correlated features

lessons.title: Spend a tuning budget deliberately
lessons.explain: Hyperparameter search is an experiment with a finite budget. Start with a defensible range based on model behavior, record all trials, and choose the selection metric before inspecting results. Random search can explore broad spaces efficiently when only a few dimensions matter; exhaustive grids waste work on arbitrary resolution. Fix seeds for debugging while checking robustness with additional seeds where stochastic variation matters. Compare models under similar resource limits and include fit time, prediction latency, and artifact size. The best validation score is not automatically the most useful engineering choice for the intended deployment.
lessons.practice: Run a small reproducible search over tree depth, leaf size, and boosting strength using a fixed trial budget; benchmark the chosen model against the linear baseline.
lessons.deliverable: A model tournament table and resource-aware selection memo.
lessons.check: Why should an experiment log include unsuccessful and invalid trials?
lessons.answer: They explain how the search was conducted, expose fragility or configuration errors, and prevent selective reporting. Failed trials also consume the real tuning budget.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn randomized search and model selection

workedExample.title: A perfect training split is not a generalization claim
workedExample.code:
labels = [0, 0, 1, 1]
def gini(values):
    p = sum(values) / len(values)
    return 1 - p * p - (1 - p) ** 2
left, right = labels[:2], labels[2:]
parent = gini(labels)
weighted_children = (len(left) * gini(left) + len(right) * gini(right)) / len(labels)
print("parent_impurity", parent)
print("child_impurity", weighted_children)
print("training_gain", parent - weighted_children)
workedExample.explanation: Gini impurity measures the class mixture inside a node. This split creates pure leaves and maximizes the gain for these four training observations. A tree could obtain equally pure leaves by memorizing an identifier, so impurity reduction alone does not justify a useful decision boundary. Minimum leaf sizes, depth constraints and held-out comparisons limit different forms of complexity. Bagging reduces instability by averaging varied learners; boosting builds learners sequentially to improve an objective. Neither bypasses the need for a valid evaluation population.

assessment.question: A deep tree assigns every training example to a pure leaf. Which conclusion follows?
options: It will classify every future example correctly.
It has zero training classification error, but may have learned unstable or irrelevant splits.
Its predicted probabilities are necessarily calibrated.
No cross-validation is needed.
assessment.explanation: Pure leaves establish a property of the observed training labels. With enough depth, a tree can isolate individual examples and memorize noise or IDs. Future observations may follow different patterns, and a leaf containing one positive example does not establish a reliable probability of one. Evaluate on held-out data and constrain complexity based on the task and sample size.

connections.before: The baseline objective from c13 expands into piecewise decisions and ensembles.
connections.after: Feature pipelines and error analysis must evaluate the entire fitted procedure, not only the estimator.

modules.title: Evaluation: decisions, uncertainty, and calibration
modules.summary: Choose metrics and uncertainty estimates that match the decision being made.
modules.why: A model score becomes meaningful only when its population, threshold, uncertainty, and consequences are explicit.
outcomes: Select metrics from error consequences
Distinguish discrimination from calibration
Report uncertainty and subgroup limitations

project.title: A decision-focused evaluation dossier
project.brief: Evaluate a binary predictor under a stated resource limit and error-cost model, including subgroup and uncertainty analysis.
deliverables: Metric and threshold rationale
Calibration and precision-recall plots
Bootstrap interval with sampling assumptions
Slice report and explicit limitations
rubric: Threshold is selected using validation data only
Intervals respect independent sampling units
Small slices are reported with uncertainty and privacy care

pitfalls: Accuracy under severe imbalance
Bootstrap sampling the wrong unit
Treating calibration as a guarantee for every subgroup

lessons.title: Let the decision choose the metric
lessons.explain: Metrics summarize different consequences. Precision asks how often positive predictions are correct; recall asks how much of the positive population is detected. Both depend on a chosen threshold, and precision also changes with prevalence even when sensitivity and specificity remain constant. Accuracy can be dominated by the majority class. Start with the practical action: limited review capacity, missed-case cost, or a ranking task. Then select a primary metric and guardrails. A confusion matrix expressed as counts per expected number of real users often communicates tradeoffs more clearly than a single normalized score.
lessons.practice: Construct a 10,000-case confusion matrix at 1% prevalence with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity; calculate precision, recall, and workload.
lessons.deliverable: A decision memo with counts, rates, and review-capacity implications.
lessons.check: What is precision in that example?
lessons.answer: There are 90 true positives and 495 false positives, so precision is 90/585, approximately 15.4%. High sensitivity and specificity can still yield low precision at low prevalence.
lessons.videoQuery: Google machine learning crash course precision recall and class imbalance

lessons.title: Ranking and thresholds answer different questions
lessons.explain: A ranking metric asks whether positive examples tend to receive higher scores than negative examples. A deployment decision requires an operating threshold, capacity constraint, or ranking cutoff. ROC curves compare true-positive and false-positive rates; precision-recall curves make positive prediction quality and coverage more visible, especially when positives are rare. Areas under curves do not identify a safe operating point. Choose the threshold on validation data using a declared utility or constraint, then evaluate once on a held-out test. Revisit the decision rule when costs, capacity, or prevalence change, while distinguishing that update from model retraining.
lessons.practice: Plot ROC and precision-recall curves, then choose a threshold that fits a maximum of 100 manual reviews per day on validation predictions.
lessons.deliverable: Threshold-selection code and a capacity-versus-recall chart.
lessons.check: Can a model with better ROC AUC have worse precision at your chosen review capacity?
lessons.answer: Yes. AUC aggregates ranking behavior across operating points; the part of the ranking used by a specific capacity limit can be worse despite a better overall area.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn ROC and precision-recall evaluation

lessons.title: A probability must earn its interpretation
lessons.explain: A calibrated probability has a frequency interpretation: among similar predictions near 0.7, the event occurs about 70% of the time in the evaluated population. Calibration differs from ranking; a monotonic score transformation can preserve order while changing probability quality. Reliability diagrams compare predicted probabilities and observed frequencies, but conclusions depend on bin sizes and sample counts. Brier score and log loss evaluate probability predictions with different penalties. Calibration methods must be fitted on data separate from the original model training and assessed on unseen examples. Good aggregate calibration does not guarantee calibration for every subgroup or under distribution shift.
lessons.practice: Distort a classifier’s probabilities with a power transform, then compare ranking, log loss, Brier score, and reliability plots before and after calibration.
lessons.deliverable: A calibration report with per-bin sample counts.
lessons.check: If all predicted probabilities are doubled and clipped to one, will ROC AUC necessarily improve?
lessons.answer: No. A monotonic transformation generally preserves ranking, while clipping creates ties; probability calibration can worsen substantially even when ranking changes little.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn probability calibration reliability diagrams

lessons.title: Quantify how uncertain the metric is
lessons.explain: An observed metric is computed from a finite sample and can change on another sample. Bootstrap intervals approximate this variation by resampling the appropriate independent units and recomputing the statistic. If many rows belong to one patient or account, resampling individual rows can understate uncertainty; use the cluster as the unit when justified. Time dependence needs additional care. For comparing models on the same observations, paired resampling preserves the shared cases and can improve precision. An interval describes uncertainty under assumptions about the sample and procedure; it does not include every future shift, label error, or selection bias.
lessons.practice: Bootstrap a metric difference using paired predictions; repeat by row and by user on a dataset with repeated users and explain the discrepancy.
lessons.deliverable: A metric-difference interval with a clearly documented resampling unit.
lessons.check: Does a 95% confidence interval mean a 95% probability that the fixed unknown parameter lies in this realized interval?
lessons.answer: In the frequentist interpretation, 95% refers to long-run coverage of intervals generated by the procedure under its assumptions, not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter.
lessons.videoQuery: Statistical learning bootstrap confidence intervals and paired comparisons

lessons.title: Find failures hidden by averages
lessons.explain: An average can hide poor performance on important populations, rare conditions, or difficult inputs. Define slices from the application and plausible failure mechanisms, then report sample sizes alongside metrics. Tiny slices produce unstable estimates; avoid treating a noisy difference as a settled fact. Fairness criteria encode different goals and can conflict, especially when base rates differ. Select criteria with affected stakeholders and applicable requirements rather than assuming one score proves fairness. Separate diagnostic exploration from confirmatory evaluation. Finally, document which people and situations the evaluation represents and where the evidence is absent.
lessons.practice: Evaluate the project model across three justified slices, review five errors from the weakest slice, and propose one testable improvement without retuning on the final test.
lessons.deliverable: An evaluation dossier with aggregate results, slices, uncertainty, and limitations.
lessons.check: Why can equal accuracy across two groups still conceal unequal harm?
lessons.answer: Groups may have different prevalence or different false-positive and false-negative costs. Equal aggregate accuracy can coexist with very different error types, access burdens, or individual consequences.
lessons.videoQuery: NIST AI RMF measurement validity and harmful bias

workedExample.title: Choose a threshold from costs, not habit
workedExample.code:
cases = [(0.9, 1), (0.4, 1), (0.8, 0), (0.2, 0)]
for threshold in (0.5, 0.3):
    tp = sum(score >= threshold and label == 1 for score, label in cases)
    fp = sum(score >= threshold and label == 0 for score, label in cases)
    fn = sum(score < threshold and label == 1 for score, label in cases)
    tn = len(cases) - tp - fp - fn
    cost = fp + 8 * fn
    print(f"threshold={threshold:.1f} TP={tp} FP={fp} TN={tn} FN={fn} cost={cost}")
workedExample.expected:
threshold=0.5 TP=1 FP=1 TN=1 FN=1 cost=9
threshold=0.3 TP=2 FP=1 TN=1 FN=0 cost=1
workedExample.explanation: Lowering the threshold catches the second positive case without introducing another false positive in this tiny example. Because missing a positive is assigned eight times the cost of a false alarm, the decision cost drops. These costs are assumptions that must come from the actual decision context. The sample is illustrative and must not be used to infer real-world performance. In practice, choose thresholds using validation data, report uncertainty and capacity constraints, and evaluate the final policy on appropriately held-out cases.

assessment.question: A model has high ROC-AUC. What must still be established before choosing a deployment threshold?
options: Nothing; a high AUC fixes the threshold at 0.5.
That every predicted score is rounded to an integer.
Error costs, capacity, population conditions and performance of the chosen policy.
That accuracy is exactly equal to AUC.
assessment.explanation: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across thresholds; it does not choose a particular operating point. Deployment requires a policy with acceptable false alarms, missed cases, workload and costs in the relevant population. If scores are interpreted as probabilities, calibration also matters. Threshold selection itself is part of model development and should not repeatedly consume the final test set.

connections.before: Probability and statistical uncertainty become concrete decisions with asymmetric consequences.
connections.after: Monitoring and product experiments must track the deployed policy, not only a model-level score.

project.title: A raw-record-to-prediction pipeline
project.brief: Build a single artifact that accepts documented raw records, validates them, transforms features, and returns predictions.
deliverables: Input schema and failure policy
Cross-validated preprocessing pipeline
Reproducible artifact and batch inference command
Tests for missing and unseen categories

Reloaded artifact reproduces predictions within tolerance
Bad records produce explicit failures or documented fallbacks

pitfalls: Target encoding before cross-validation
Training-serving skew
Silently accepting changed units or categories

lessons.title: Features are information available at a time
lessons.explain: A feature is useful only if it can be obtained when the prediction must be made. Distinguish event time, recording time, and processing time: a field can describe an earlier event yet arrive too late for the decision. A target proxy may leak the answer through business workflows, post-outcome actions, or joined tables. Write a feature contract naming source, units, missingness, and availability. Reconstruct training examples as they would have appeared at prediction time. High offline performance is suspicious when a feature encodes decisions that happen after the outcome or depends on data that will not exist in service.
lessons.practice: Audit ten candidate features for a loan-default or support-escalation predictor; label availability time and remove post-outcome fields before comparing validation scores.
lessons.deliverable: A feature availability table and leakage audit.
lessons.check: A refund-issued field is highly predictive of a complaint being valid. Can it be used when the complaint is first submitted?
lessons.answer: Only if the refund is already known at that decision time, which is usually false. A later refund can encode the outcome or investigation and would leak future information.
lessons.videoQuery: Google machine learning crash course data leakage feature engineering

lessons.title: Fit transformations inside the evaluation loop
lessons.explain: Imputers, scalers, encoders, and feature selectors learn facts from data. Those fitted facts belong to model training, even if the transformation never reads the target. Learning them from evaluation rows contaminates the measurement. A pipeline makes each cross-validation fold fit its transformations on that fold’s training portion and apply them unchanged to its validation portion. Different column types require different policies, so use a column transformer or equivalent explicit composition. Preserve feature names and units where possible; otherwise a seemingly harmless change in column order can silently alter the meaning of every prediction.
lessons.practice: Build numeric and categorical preprocessing with imputation, scaling, and one-hot encoding inside a cross-validated model pipeline.
lessons.deliverable: A single pipeline with a fold-level leakage check.
lessons.check: Should the median used for imputation be computed once on the entire dataset before cross-validation?
lessons.answer: No. Each training fold must compute its own median, then apply that median to its validation fold. The final fitted pipeline learns its median from the full training partition only.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn pipelines common pitfalls and column transformer

lessons.title: Missing and unknown are different states
lessons.explain: A missing value means a field was absent or unobserved; an unknown category means a valid field contains a value not seen during fitting. These situations can have different meanings and should not collapse accidentally into the same representation. Missingness may be informative because collection depends on the process or outcome, but that relationship can change. Decide whether invalid inputs should be rejected, routed for review, or handled with a documented fallback. Validate ranges, units, types, and required fields before prediction. Monitoring should count these events so that graceful handling does not hide a deteriorating data pipeline.
lessons.practice: Create inference cases with a missing age, unseen category, impossible negative count, numeric string, and changed unit; test the intended behavior for each.
lessons.deliverable: An input-validation matrix and executable edge-case tests.
lessons.check: Why is replacing every missing numeric value with zero potentially harmful?
lessons.answer: Zero may be a valid and meaningful observation, so the replacement conflates missingness with an actual value and can distort distributions. A training-fitted imputer and optional missingness indicator are often more defensible.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn imputation and encoding unknown categories

lessons.title: Target-derived features need out-of-fold construction
lessons.explain: Target encoding summarizes how the target varies by category, which can be useful for high-cardinality inputs. It can also reveal an example’s own label if computed naively. Out-of-fold construction creates training features using summaries from other folds, while a final encoder fitted on the training set transforms new data. Smoothing pulls sparse categories toward a broader prior and reduces variance. Time-dependent settings require encodings that respect time as well as label separation. Compare with simpler encodings first; a complex feature that wins on a contaminated validation protocol teaches the wrong lesson about model quality.
lessons.practice: Generate random labels and near-unique categories; show how naive target encoding appears predictive, then implement out-of-fold encoding and compare honestly.
lessons.deliverable: A leakage demonstration with naive and cross-fitted results.
lessons.check: What should happen on genuinely random labels when target encoding is evaluated without leakage?
lessons.answer: Held-out performance should remain near the appropriate chance or dummy baseline, apart from sampling variation. A large stable gain is evidence to investigate the protocol or data.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn target encoder cross fitting

lessons.title: One artifact, many consistent predictions
lessons.explain: A saved model is incomplete if its preprocessing, feature order, label mapping, and dependency assumptions are missing. Package the transformation pipeline and estimator together, record training-data identity and configuration, and validate a small set of reference inputs after reloading. Exact bitwise reproducibility may not hold across hardware or library versions, so define numerical tolerances appropriate to the use case. Serialization formats can execute code when loaded, so only load artifacts from trusted sources. A batch interface should state how it handles rejected rows and preserve identifiers, allowing downstream users to join predictions back to the correct records.
lessons.practice: Save and reload the project pipeline, compare reference predictions, and run a batch command on records containing both valid and invalid rows.
lessons.deliverable: A versioned pipeline artifact, model manifest, and inference report.
lessons.check: Why is saving only the fitted estimator insufficient after training with a scaler and encoder?
lessons.answer: Inference must reproduce the fitted transformations and feature mapping. Recomputing or omitting them changes the inputs the estimator sees and can silently invalidate predictions.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn model persistence security and reproducibility

workedExample.title: Fit preprocessing where learning is allowed
workedExample.code:
train = [0.0, 2.0]
test = [100.0]
training_center = sum(train) / len(train)
leaky_center = sum(train + test) / len(train + test)
def center(values, learned_center):
    return [x - learned_center for x in values]
print("training_center", training_center)
print("train", center(train, training_center))
print("test", center(test, training_center))
print("leaky_center", leaky_center)
workedExample.explanation: Centering appears harmless because it does not use labels, but the center is still a learned property of the observed data. Computing it on the full dataset lets the held-out distribution influence the fitted procedure. The correct transformation learns its center from training data and applies that same value to every later input. Cross-validation requires a separate fit inside each training fold. A pipeline helps enforce this boundary; it does not automatically fix an invalid feature, split or target definition.

assessment.question: A scaler uses no labels. Is fitting it on train plus test data always safe?
options: Yes; only labels can leak information.
Yes, if the scaler has fewer parameters than the model.
No; scaling is never allowed in machine learning.
No; learning distribution statistics from the holdout can contaminate evaluation.
assessment.explanation: A transformation can learn information without using labels. Imputation, scaling, vocabulary construction and feature selection can all adapt to the held-out distribution. Fit transformations within the allowed training boundary and apply them unchanged to validation or test inputs. A special transductive setting may define different information access, but that must be an explicit evaluation design, not an accidental shortcut.

connections.before: Earlier preprocessing choices become fitted objects with explicit information boundaries.
connections.after: Training, cross-validation and online serving must all preserve the same transformation contract.
