modules.summary: Explore geometry, compression, clustering, and similarity search without mistaking patterns for truth.
modules.why: Modern retrieval systems depend on distance and representation; unsupervised methods reveal how those choices shape every result.
outcomes: Choose and critique distance functions
Use PCA and clustering with explicit assumptions
Evaluate a simple nearest-neighbor retrieval system

project.title: A measured similarity explorer
project.brief: Build a small record or document similarity explorer with a labeled relevance set and a comparison of representations.
deliverables: Distance and scaling rationale
PCA and clustering exploration
Top-k retrieval evaluation with failure examples
rubric: Training transforms are isolated from evaluation
Clusters are described as model-dependent partitions
Retrieval is judged against explicit relevance labels

pitfalls: Assuming clusters are naturally existing categories
Using raw Euclidean distance across incompatible scales
Treating a two-dimensional visualization as proof

lessons.title: Distance is a modeling decision
lessons.explain: Nearest-neighbor methods replace an explicit fitted equation with a question: which stored examples are most similar to this input? Similarity depends on representation, scaling, and distance. Euclidean distance measures absolute separation; cosine similarity compares direction and is often useful when vector magnitude is not the intended signal. Normalizing vectors changes the question being asked. In high dimensions, distances may become less discriminative, and irrelevant features can overwhelm useful structure. Before choosing an index or algorithm, write a concrete example of two items that should be close and two that should be far apart under the application’s notion of relevance.
lessons.practice: Create vectors with mismatched units and compare nearest neighbors before scaling, after scaling, and with cosine similarity; explain three changed matches.
lessons.deliverable: A distance-choice notebook with hand-calculated examples.
lessons.check: Can two vectors have cosine similarity one but very different Euclidean distance?
lessons.answer: Yes. Any two nonzero vectors pointing in the same direction have cosine similarity one, even if their lengths differ greatly; Euclidean distance reflects that magnitude difference.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn nearest neighbors distance metrics

lessons.title: PCA compresses variance, not meaning
lessons.explain: Principal component analysis finds orthogonal directions that capture the greatest variance in centered data. Projecting onto a few directions can compress information, reduce noise, or make patterns easier to inspect. Variance is not the same as predictive value: a low-variance direction might contain the signal relevant to the target. Feature scaling changes which directions dominate, so choose it intentionally. Fit PCA on training data and apply the learned projection to evaluation data. A two-dimensional projection necessarily discards structure; visually separated groups are hypotheses to investigate, and overlapping points do not prove the original data are inseparable.
lessons.practice: Apply PCA to correlated synthetic measurements, compare scaled and unscaled results, and measure reconstruction error as components are added.
lessons.deliverable: Explained-variance and reconstruction-error plots with a scaling explanation.
lessons.check: Does retaining 95% of feature variance guarantee retaining 95% of predictive information?
lessons.answer: No. PCA ignores the target. Predictive signal can lie in low-variance directions, so downstream performance must be evaluated separately.
lessons.videoQuery: MIT linear algebra principal components and singular value decomposition

lessons.title: Clustering answers the question you encode
lessons.explain: Clustering groups observations according to an algorithm’s representation and objective. K-means minimizes squared distance to centroids, favoring roughly compact groups under Euclidean geometry. Density-based approaches can identify irregular dense regions and label some points as noise, but their parameters encode what counts as dense. A numerical cluster score does not establish that the groups correspond to useful human categories. Inspect stability under reasonable preprocessing choices and perturbations, then ask whether the groups support a real decision. If labels already define the decision, supervised evaluation may be more appropriate than treating clustering as a substitute for labeled evidence.
lessons.practice: Compare k-means and a density-based method on blobs, concentric shapes, and uneven-density data; inspect where each objective succeeds or fails.
lessons.deliverable: A clustering assumptions gallery with stability observations.
lessons.check: Why might k-means fail on two concentric rings?
lessons.answer: Its distance-to-centroid objective favors convex Voronoi regions. Points on each ring surround a similar center, so the desired ring grouping is poorly represented by centroid-based partitions.
lessons.videoQuery: Scikit-learn clustering comparison and assumptions

lessons.title: Measure whether retrieval finds what matters
lessons.explain: Retrieval returns a short list from a larger collection, so evaluation must represent the queries and relevance judgments that matter. Build a query set with one or more acceptable results, including ambiguous and no-answer cases. Recall at k measures how much relevant material appears in the top k results under the labeling scheme; ranking metrics also reward placing useful items earlier. A missing relevant label can make a good result look wrong, so inspect disagreements. Keep development queries separate from final evaluation queries, and compare against a simple lexical or exact-match baseline before adding more complex representations.
lessons.practice: Create twenty realistic queries for a small corpus, label relevant items, and compare token-overlap ranking with a numeric or vector representation.
lessons.deliverable: A query-relevance file, top-k metrics, and five failure analyses.
lessons.check: Why can retrieval recall appear worse after discovering additional relevant documents?
lessons.answer: The denominator of relevant items increases. Earlier labels were incomplete, so apparent performance depended on the annotation process as well as the retrieval system.
lessons.videoQuery: Information retrieval evaluation precision recall ranking

lessons.title: Indexing trades accuracy for speed and memory
lessons.explain: Exact nearest-neighbor search compares a query with every candidate, which is a valuable correctness baseline but can become expensive as the collection grows. Approximate indexes reduce work by organizing or compressing vectors, accepting that some true neighbors may be missed. Distinguish index recall against exact neighbors from task relevance: matching exact vector neighbors does not prove the representation retrieves useful information. Benchmark build time, memory, update behavior, and query latency alongside quality. A small corpus may not need an approximate index at all; select infrastructure after measuring the workload rather than because a particular database is fashionable.
lessons.practice: Benchmark exact search on a growing local corpus, then compare one approximate configuration if available; report both exact-neighbor recall and labeled query relevance.
lessons.deliverable: A similarity explorer report with quality, memory, and latency tradeoffs.
lessons.check: If an approximate index has 99% neighbor recall, does the product have 99% answer accuracy?
lessons.answer: No. Neighbor recall concerns agreement with exact vector search. Relevance, missing documents, downstream generation, and the correctness of answers are separate stages with separate errors.
lessons.videoQuery: FAISS similarity search tradeoffs and evaluation

workedExample.title: Distance encodes what counts as similar
workedExample.expected:
A: dot=2.000 cosine=1.000
B: dot=10.000 cosine=0.707
dot_winner B
cosine_winner A
workedExample.explanation: Raw dot product rewards magnitude as well as alignment. Cosine similarity normalizes magnitudes and compares direction, so the two metrics rank these documents differently. Neither is universally correct: vector norms may carry useful information, or may reflect an irrelevant scale effect. Zero vectors need an explicit policy because cosine is undefined there. An embedding model’s intended metric and a labeled retrieval evaluation should guide the choice. Geometric proximity is not itself proof of semantic relevance or factual support.

assessment.question: Changing from dot product to cosine changes retrieval rankings. Why?
options: Cosine removes vector magnitude from the comparison, while raw dot product includes it.
Cosine always ranks documents alphabetically.
Dot product cannot be used on embeddings.
The two metrics are identical for every pair of nonzero vectors.
assessment.explanation: For nonzero vectors, cosine divides the dot product by the product of their lengths. Rankings can change when candidate norms differ. If all candidate vectors are normalized and the query is fixed, the rankings may coincide. Choose the metric based on the embedding design and observed retrieval quality, and evaluate whether normalization discards a useful or harmful signal.

connections.before: Linear algebra provides the geometry; pipelines determine which representations are compared.
connections.after: RAG inherits retrieval’s metric choices and therefore needs evaluation before generation is added.

modules.title: Neural networks from composition and gradients
modules.summary: Derive a small neural network before relying on an automatic differentiation framework.
modules.why: Understanding the computation graph makes shapes, gradients, activations, and training failures debuggable.
outcomes: Explain why nonlinear composition expands model capacity
Trace gradients through a small network
Diagnose basic optimization and generalization failures

project.title: A tiny neural network you can explain
project.brief: Implement a two-layer classifier with NumPy, verify gradients, and compare it with a linear baseline on controlled data.
deliverables: Forward and backward passes
Numerical gradient check
Learning curves and linear-baseline comparison
rubric: Shapes are documented for every tensor
Gradients agree with finite differences
The network can overfit a tiny clean subset before full training

pitfalls: Stacking linear layers without nonlinearities
Confusing failed optimization with underfitting capacity
Changing many training settings at once

lessons.title: A network is a composition of functions
lessons.explain: A neural network composes simple parameterized operations into a more flexible function. An affine layer transforms a vector with a matrix and bias; an activation introduces nonlinearity. Without nonlinear activations, multiple affine layers collapse into a single affine transformation, regardless of depth. Hidden units can construct intermediate features useful for the final task, but they do not come with guaranteed human meanings. Track shapes before calculating values: batch size, input width, hidden width, and output width determine valid matrix products. This habit turns many mysterious framework errors into ordinary checks about the function you intended to compute.
lessons.practice: Implement an affine-ReLU-affine forward pass in NumPy; annotate shapes and demonstrate that two linear layers collapse into one.
lessons.deliverable: A shape-annotated forward function and algebraic collapse demonstration.
lessons.check: Why can an affine-only network not solve XOR exactly?
lessons.answer: Its composition remains affine, producing a linear decision boundary. XOR classes are not linearly separable, so at least a suitable nonlinearity or nonlinear features are needed.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning multilayer perceptrons

lessons.title: Backpropagation is the chain rule organized
lessons.explain: Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule through a computation graph. Each operation knows how a small change in its input affects its output; the backward pass combines these local derivatives with the loss sensitivity arriving from later operations. When a value feeds multiple branches, contributions to its gradient add. The algorithm computes derivatives, not an update rule: an optimizer decides how parameters change afterward. Work through a tiny graph numerically before implementing matrices, then compare analytic derivatives with finite differences. A gradient can be mathematically correct while learning still fails because the loss, data, or update schedule is unsuitable.
lessons.practice: Differentiate a scalar graph by hand, then implement gradients for a two-layer network and check selected parameters with central finite differences.
lessons.deliverable: A hand-derived graph and automated gradient-check output.
lessons.check: If one parameter affects the loss through two independent paths, what happens to its gradient?
lessons.answer: The chain-rule contributions from both paths are added. Ignoring either path produces an incomplete derivative and usually an incorrect training update.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning backpropagation and computation graphs

lessons.title: Initialization and activation control signal flow
lessons.explain: Training depends on signals moving forward and gradients moving backward at usable scales. Saturating activations can produce very small derivatives for large-magnitude inputs. ReLU avoids saturation on its positive side but has zero derivative on the negative side, so some units can become inactive. Initializing every hidden unit identically preserves symmetry and prevents them from learning different features. Variance-aware initialization aims to keep activation scales from exploding or shrinking through layers. These are practical consequences of composition and multiplication, not magic defaults. Inspect activation and gradient distributions when depth or a new architecture makes optimization unstable.
lessons.practice: Compare zero, very large, and variance-aware initialization on the same small network; record activation distributions, gradient norms, and learning curves.
lessons.deliverable: An initialization experiment with an explanation of one failed run.
lessons.check: Why is initializing all hidden weights to zero problematic even when the output loss has a gradient?
lessons.answer: Hidden units begin identically and receive identical updates, so symmetry prevents them from learning distinct features. Some architectures also block useful gradients under zero initialization.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning numerical stability initialization

lessons.title: Optimization noise and generalization differ
lessons.explain: Mini-batch training estimates the full-data gradient from a subset of examples. This makes updates cheaper and introduces sampling noise, which interacts with batch size, learning rate, and data order. Momentum accumulates a direction over time, while adaptive optimizers adjust updates using gradient statistics. None removes the need to choose a sensible learning rate or validate generalization. Plot training and validation losses separately: falling training loss with rising validation loss suggests a different problem from losses that both remain high. First make the network fit a tiny clean subset; this tests basic capacity and implementation before more elaborate regularization experiments.
lessons.practice: Train the same network with full-batch and mini-batch updates, then compare two learning rates; verify tiny-subset overfitting first.
lessons.deliverable: A controlled optimizer comparison with training and validation curves.
lessons.check: If a sufficiently large network cannot overfit sixteen clean examples, what should you inspect before adding dropout?
lessons.answer: Check data-label alignment, forward and backward code, loss choice, learning rate, parameter updates, and activation behavior. Regularization can make fitting harder and does not fix these implementation problems.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning stochastic gradient descent and momentum

lessons.title: Capacity must earn its cost
lessons.explain: A flexible network can approximate complicated patterns, including noise and accidental correlations. Generalization requires evaluating how its learned function behaves on examples outside training. Weight decay discourages large parameters; early stopping limits the optimization trajectory; dropout perturbs intermediate units during training. These mechanisms are different and should not be treated as interchangeable switches. Use small ablations that change one meaningful choice at a time, and compare with a simpler model on the same split. Explain whether the gain comes from representation, additional tuning, or data changes. A more complex model is justified only by an improvement that matters for the task.
lessons.practice: Complete the NumPy network project with a linear baseline, one regularization experiment, and a short report identifying capacity, optimization, and generalization separately.
lessons.deliverable: A neural-network experiment report with reproducible configuration.
lessons.check: Training error is low and validation error high. Does this prove that more hidden units are needed?
lessons.answer: No. The gap is consistent with overfitting or a split/data issue. More capacity may worsen it; inspect the protocol, regularization, data coverage, and simpler alternatives.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning underfitting overfitting weight decay

workedExample.title: Backpropagation is the chain rule with bookkeeping
workedExample.code:
x, w, v, target = 2.0, 1.0, 3.0, 5.0
z = w * x
hidden = max(0.0, z)
prediction = v * hidden
loss = (prediction - target) ** 2
d_prediction = 2 * (prediction - target)
d_v = d_prediction * hidden
d_hidden = d_prediction * v
d_z = d_hidden * (1.0 if z > 0 else 0.0)
d_w = d_z * x
print("prediction", prediction, "loss", loss)
print("gradient_w", d_w, "gradient_v", d_v)
workedExample.explanation: Each backward quantity answers a local sensitivity question and is multiplied by the derivative of the operation immediately before it. The hidden activation contributes a factor of zero or one for this ReLU away from its kink. This makes the dependency graph explicit: the loss depends on v directly through the hidden value, while it depends on w through multiplication and activation. Automatic differentiation performs this bookkeeping at scale, but a tiny manual trace helps identify shape errors, disconnected parameters and zero-gradient regimes.

assessment.question: If z is strictly negative in this ReLU example, what is the gradient contribution through that activation?
options: One, because every neuron must learn equally.
Zero, because the activation is locally constant in that region.
Undefined at every negative value.
Equal to the learning rate.
assessment.explanation: ReLU is max(0,z), so it is constant and has derivative zero for strictly negative z. At z=0 it is nondifferentiable and implementations choose a convention. A zero local derivative blocks the gradient through that path for that example; it is not proof that the full network is globally optimal or that every parameter has zero gradient.

connections.before: The chain rule and linear transformations combine into a trainable composition.
connections.after: PyTorch’s autograd can now be checked against a small computation you understand manually.

modules.summary: Use tensors, automatic differentiation, data loaders, and checkpoints to make experiments reproducible.
modules.why: A training framework saves arithmetic work; the engineer still owns data correctness, optimization state, and evaluation behavior.

Debug tensor shape, device, and gradient errors

lessons.title: Tensors, devices, and automatic differentiation
lessons.explain: A tensor stores numbers with a shape, data type, and device. Operations build a computation graph when gradient tracking is enabled; backward traversal computes derivatives for requested parameters. Automatic differentiation applies exact chain rules to the implemented operations, subject to floating-point arithmetic, rather than estimating gradients with finite differences. The graph can break when values are detached or converted into unrelated arrays. Device and dtype mismatches often reveal that inputs and parameters were created through inconsistent paths. Begin on CPU with a tiny example, inspect gradients explicitly, and move to accelerators only after the function behaves as intended.
lessons.practice: Recreate the NumPy network in PyTorch, compare forward outputs and parameter gradients on the same small batch, and deliberately diagnose one dtype mismatch.
lessons.deliverable: A NumPy-versus-PyTorch parity check with shape and dtype assertions.
lessons.check: Does calling backward automatically change the model parameters?
lessons.answer: No. It computes and accumulates gradients. An optimizer step or explicit update changes parameters; gradient clearing is also a separate operation.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch tutorials tensors and automatic differentiation

lessons.title: The data loader is part of the model contract
lessons.explain: A dataset defines how examples and labels are obtained; a data loader groups them into batches and controls iteration. Shuffling training examples can improve stochastic optimization, but validation usually needs stable ordering when predictions are joined to identifiers. Variable-sized inputs require padding or a custom collation rule. Inspect a batch visually or numerically before training, checking ranges, label distribution, shape, and correspondence between input and target. Multiple loading workers can improve throughput but introduce additional randomness and resource use. A fast loader that pairs the wrong labels with examples only accelerates the production of misleading results.
lessons.practice: Implement Dataset and DataLoader objects, inspect five examples and one batch, then verify that saved identifiers still align with validation predictions.
lessons.deliverable: A data-pipeline smoke check and labeled batch summary.
lessons.check: Why can shuffling validation data cause trouble even when the metric computation itself remains correct?
lessons.answer: If predictions are later joined to labels or records by position rather than stable identifiers, shuffling can misalign them. Preserve identifiers or explicitly preserve the ordering contract.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch tutorials datasets dataloaders custom datasets

lessons.title: Write the loop in the right order
lessons.explain: A standard training step clears previous gradients, computes predictions and loss, backpropagates, and updates parameters. PyTorch accumulates gradients by default, which enables deliberate accumulation across microbatches but causes bugs when accidental. Loss reductions determine whether values represent a batch sum or mean, affecting both gradient scale and epoch reporting. Model training mode changes layers such as dropout and batch normalization; it is distinct from enabling gradient tracking. Keep logging separate from the graph where appropriate, and verify that parameters actually change after an update. A tiny-subset overfit check remains one of the quickest ways to detect a broken loop.
lessons.practice: Write an explicit training loop with assertions for finite loss and nonzero parameter updates; demonstrate intentional versus accidental gradient accumulation.
lessons.deliverable: A tested training step and loss aggregation function.
lessons.check: Why can averaging per-batch mean losses without weights produce the wrong epoch loss?
lessons.answer: If batch sizes differ, especially the final batch, equal weighting overweights smaller batches. Weight each batch mean by its example count, then divide by the total number of examples.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch optimization loop zero_grad backward step

lessons.title: Validation is a separate computation mode
lessons.explain: Validation should estimate performance without updating the model or consuming unnecessary memory for gradients. Set evaluation mode so dropout and batch normalization behave appropriately, and disable gradient recording for the validation computation. These are separate controls: evaluation mode alone does not prevent graph construction. Aggregate metrics according to their definitions; not every metric can be averaged correctly across batches. Keep the validation data outside optimizer updates and document how often it is consulted for early stopping or selection. Compare training and validation input transformations carefully, since random augmentations appropriate for learning may make evaluation noisy or unrealistic.
lessons.practice: Implement an evaluation function, test that parameters remain unchanged, and compare dropout outputs in train and eval modes on repeated identical inputs.
lessons.deliverable: A validation routine with state-preservation and aggregation tests.
lessons.check: Does torch.no_grad() automatically disable dropout?
lessons.answer: No. It disables gradient recording. Dropout behavior is controlled by model.train() and model.eval(), so validation typically requires both evaluation mode and disabled gradient tracking.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch tutorials model eval no_grad inference

lessons.title: A checkpoint is a recoverable experiment state
lessons.explain: Saving parameters supports inference, but resuming training also requires optimizer state, schedule position, training progress, and the configuration that constructed the model. Random-state restoration may be needed for closer reproducibility, while hardware and some operations can still introduce nondeterminism. Save a best-validation checkpoint separately from the latest resumable state, and record how each was selected. After loading, verify predictions on fixed reference inputs and test a short continuation run. Treat checkpoints as trusted artifacts: loading arbitrary serialized objects can be unsafe. A compact manifest connects weights with preprocessing, label mapping, code version, and the evidence supporting their use.
lessons.practice: Interrupt a short run after two epochs, resume it, compare with an uninterrupted run under controlled settings, and export a separate inference command.
lessons.deliverable: A restartable project with checkpoint manifest and parity report.
lessons.check: Why can resuming with the same weights but a fresh momentum optimizer produce a different trajectory?
lessons.answer: Momentum and adaptive statistics summarize previous gradients. Resetting them changes future updates even when parameters and the next batch are identical.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch saving loading models general checkpoints

workedExample.title: Gradient accumulation is explicit state
workedExample.code:
import torch
w = torch.tensor([1.0], requires_grad=True)
loss = ((2 * w - 6) ** 2).sum()
loss.backward()
print("first", w.grad.item())
second_loss = ((2 * w - 6) ** 2).sum()
second_loss.backward()
print("accumulated", w.grad.item())
w.grad.zero_()
print("cleared", w.grad.item())
workedExample.explanation: Backward adds into a parameter’s gradient buffer; it does not silently reset it. The two freshly constructed forward graphs have the same derivative at the unchanged weight, so their contributions accumulate. A normal optimizer loop clears gradients at the intended update boundary, commonly with optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True). Deliberate microbatch accumulation is useful, but the loss scaling and update schedule must match the intended effective objective. Separately, eval mode changes layers such as dropout; it does not disable autograd by itself.

assessment.question: Calling model.eval() guarantees that parameter gradients will not be recorded. Is that correct?
options: Yes; eval mode and no_grad are the same mechanism.
Yes, but only for linear layers.
No; eval changes relevant layer behavior, while no_grad or inference_mode controls gradient recording.
No; evaluation mode always doubles gradients.
assessment.explanation: Evaluation mode changes modules with different training and inference behavior, such as dropout and batch normalization. Gradient recording is a separate concern controlled by autograd context managers and tensor requirements. Inference commonly uses both model.eval() and an appropriate no-grad context. Keeping these mechanisms separate makes validation reproducible and avoids unnecessary graphs without assuming one command does everything.

connections.before: Manual gradient paths become an automated training loop with mutable optimizer and gradient state.
connections.after: Reliable checkpoints, transfer learning and serving all depend on controlling that state.

modules.title: Computer vision through transfer and invariance
modules.summary: Use images to study representation, augmentation, transfer learning, and real-world shift.
modules.why: Vision makes the gap between dataset performance and operational behavior visible through lighting, backgrounds, duplicates, and acquisition changes.
outcomes: Explain convolution and useful invariances
Adapt a pretrained model with a measured baseline
Audit visual datasets for leakage and domain shift

project.title: A robust small-data image classifier
project.brief: Train a modest classifier on an openly licensed image dataset and test one realistic acquisition shift.
deliverables: Dataset and license note
Frozen-backbone and fine-tuning comparison
Class and shift evaluation
Error gallery with mitigation hypotheses
rubric: Near-duplicate or source groups do not cross splits
Augmentations preserve task labels
Claims distinguish in-distribution accuracy from shifted performance

pitfalls: Random splitting near-duplicate images
Using augmentations that change the label
Assuming pretrained weights remove dataset bias

lessons.title: Convolution encodes a reusable local operation
lessons.explain: An image is an array whose nearby values often have related meanings. A convolutional layer applies the same learned local filter at many positions, sharing parameters and producing spatial feature maps. Stride changes sampling density, padding changes boundary handling, and successive layers enlarge the effective receptive field. These design choices express useful assumptions about locality and repeated visual patterns, but they do not guarantee invariance to every transformation. Track channels and spatial dimensions explicitly. A small hand-worked convolution shows what the operation computes before a pretrained network turns it into thousands of learned filters.
lessons.practice: Compute one small convolution by hand, verify it with PyTorch, and track output shapes through a two-layer image classifier.
lessons.deliverable: A convolution worksheet and shape-checked minimal model.
lessons.check: Does increasing stride usually preserve the same spatial resolution?
lessons.answer: No. Larger stride samples fewer positions and usually reduces output spatial dimensions, with the exact size depending on kernel, padding, dilation, and input dimensions.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning convolutions padding stride

lessons.title: Split images by the process that generated them
lessons.explain: Images are not necessarily independent examples. Multiple frames from one video, scans from one patient, or near-duplicates from one source can share strong signals. Random row splitting can place almost identical content in training and evaluation, exaggerating generalization. Split by the unit relevant to deployment, such as subject, source, location, or time. Inspect labels and class definitions because ambiguous visual categories create a limit on attainable agreement. Record license and consent constraints before collecting or redistributing images. A small carefully audited dataset can teach more about reliable evaluation than a much larger collection with unknown provenance.
lessons.practice: Create a dataset inventory including class, source, and group identifiers; inspect duplicate candidates and construct a group-aware train/validation/test split.
lessons.deliverable: A dataset card and split audit with sample images.
lessons.check: Why is a random frame split unsuitable for evaluating performance on new videos?
lessons.answer: Neighboring frames share scene, subject, and acquisition information. Training can effectively see the evaluation content, so the split measures interpolation within known videos rather than transfer to new ones.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning data management and dataset splits

lessons.title: Transfer learning reuses a representation
lessons.explain: A pretrained model has learned a representation from an earlier objective and dataset. A frozen-backbone baseline trains only a new prediction head, offering a cheap way to test whether those features transfer. Fine-tuning updates some or all of the backbone and can adapt representations, but it introduces more parameters, compute, and overfitting risk. Match input normalization and resolution to the pretrained model’s documented expectations. Check weight licenses and provenance, and compare with a simple baseline. Pretraining does not guarantee suitability for a new domain; medical, scientific, or unusual imagery can differ substantially from common training distributions.
lessons.practice: Train a frozen-backbone classifier, then fine-tune the last block with a smaller learning rate; compare validation quality, time, and memory.
lessons.deliverable: A transfer-learning comparison with documented preprocessing.
lessons.check: Why can fine-tuning every layer immediately with a large learning rate harm performance?
lessons.answer: Large updates can disrupt useful pretrained representations before the new task has supplied stable gradients, especially with little data. A smaller rate or staged unfreezing may be more appropriate.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch transfer learning tutorial frozen features fine tuning

lessons.title: Augmentation asserts a label-preserving symmetry
lessons.explain: Data augmentation changes training inputs while retaining labels, asserting that the transformation should not alter the target. That assertion is task-specific. Horizontal flips may be harmless for some object categories but invalid for text, laterality, or certain diagnostic labels. Strong crops can remove the relevant object entirely. Apply random augmentation only where it reflects plausible variation, and use a stable evaluation pipeline. Compare one augmentation policy against a baseline rather than assuming more distortion is better. Augmentation can improve robustness to chosen transformations, but it cannot substitute for representative data or establish reliability under unrelated distribution shifts.
lessons.practice: Test a small set of candidate augmentations visually, reject label-changing ones, and compare one justified policy with no augmentation.
lessons.deliverable: An augmentation policy card with examples and an ablation result.
lessons.check: Would rotating handwritten digits arbitrarily always preserve labels?
lessons.answer: No. Some rotations change or obscure digit identity, such as certain 6 and 9 examples. The permitted transformation range must reflect the task and labeling convention.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch torchvision transforms data augmentation

lessons.title: Evaluate the acquisition conditions, not only the class
lessons.explain: A classifier may rely on background, lighting, resolution, or acquisition artifacts that correlate with labels in the training set. Build an error gallery containing high-confidence mistakes, ambiguous cases, and examples from a deliberately different acquisition condition. Measure class-wise performance and calibration where sample sizes permit, and report the size of each slice. A synthetic corruption test is useful but represents only that particular stressor, not universal robustness. Turn observations into hypotheses that can be checked with new data or controlled changes. State where the classifier should abstain or request human review instead of presenting every output as equally trustworthy.
lessons.practice: Evaluate the final model on one documented shift such as lower resolution or a separate source; review errors and compare against in-distribution results.
lessons.deliverable: A vision project report with shift results and an error gallery.
lessons.check: Does strong performance on blurred images prove robustness to a new hospital scanner or camera location?
lessons.answer: No. Blur is one controlled perturbation. A new acquisition domain can alter many other properties, labels, and population characteristics that require representative evaluation.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning computer vision deployment and monitoring

workedExample.title: Augmentation can accidentally create train–test overlap
workedExample.code:
images = ["photo_A", "photo_B", "photo_C"]
augmented = [(image, transform) for image in images for transform in ("original", "flip")]
bad_train = augmented[::2]
bad_test = augmented[1::2]
train_sources = {source for source, _ in bad_train}
test_sources = {source for source, _ in bad_test}
print("overlap", sorted(train_sources & test_sources))
good_train_sources = set(images[:2])
good_test_sources = set(images[2:])
print("split_before_augmentation", good_train_sources.isdisjoint(good_test_sources))
workedExample.explanation: The bad split puts an original image in training and a transformed version of the same source in testing. It can measure recognition of nearly the same content instead of transfer to new source images. Split source identities before creating training augmentations, and preserve a meaningful evaluation policy. Larger groups such as a patient, video, scene or capture session may require an even higher grouping level. An augmentation must also preserve the intended label; flipping a directional symbol may change its meaning.

assessment.question: When should training augmentation normally be applied in a supervised image workflow?
options: Before the split, so every augmented view is independently randomized.
Only to the final test set.
Whenever it increases the apparent sample count, regardless of meaning.
After splitting independent source groups, and only where the transformation preserves the task label.
assessment.explanation: Augmented views are not independent new source observations. Splitting them separately can put related content on both sides of the evaluation boundary. Create the split at the appropriate source group first, then apply label-preserving training transformations. Keep validation and test processing aligned with the intended deployment question and document any deliberate test-time augmentation separately.

connections.before: Training-loop correctness is necessary before adapting a model to a new visual distribution.
connections.after: The same source-identity reasoning applies to documents, conversations and other correlated data.

modules.title: Language models from tokens to transformers
modules.summary: Reconstruct the operations behind a small language model, then connect their limits to practical text applications.
modules.why: A fluent interface can hide a probabilistic sequence model. Understanding the mechanism makes evaluation, cost, and failure analysis more concrete.
outcomes: Trace text through tokens, embeddings, attention, and output probabilities
Train and inspect a tiny causal model on a licensed toy corpus
Distinguish a next-token objective from factual reliability

project.title: A tiny language model with an honest report
project.brief: Build a character-level or small-vocabulary next-token model whose training, masking, sampling, and failures you can explain. Use a small openly licensed corpus and CPU-friendly dimensions.
deliverables: Tokenizer round-trip tests and a corpus license note
Shape-checked causal attention implementation
Training and held-out loss curves
Samples under several decoding settings and a limitations report
rubric: Held-out text does not influence vocabulary or model selection without disclosure
A test proves future tokens cannot affect an earlier prediction
Probability outputs and sampling behavior are explained without claiming factual understanding

pitfalls: Treating tokens as words in every language
Assuming attention weights explain model reasoning
Training on unlicensed private text or confusing low loss with truth

lessons.title: A tokenizer chooses the units of prediction
lessons.explain: A language model predicts units chosen by a tokenizer, rather than directly predicting human ideas. A character vocabulary is easy to inspect but produces long sequences; subword methods trade vocabulary size against sequence length and can represent unfamiliar words as pieces. The same sentence can use different token counts under different tokenizers, affecting context capacity and cost. Build a reversible encoding before relying on a library, and specify how unknown symbols are handled. Fit any learned vocabulary using the intended training data. Tokenization is a representation decision with consequences for multilingual text, code, spacing, and rare names.
lessons.practice: Build a character tokenizer for a small public-domain text. Test encode/decode round trips for spaces, punctuation, Unicode characters, and an unseen symbol; compare lengths with a documented subword tokenizer if available.
lessons.deliverable: Tokenizer code, round-trip tests, and a short comparison of vocabulary and sequence length.
lessons.check: Why is a fixed number of tokens not a fixed number of words, especially across languages?
lessons.answer: Tokens may be characters, bytes, subword pieces, or whole words. Vocabulary and text structure determine how many pieces represent a word, so token-to-word ratios vary by tokenizer, language, and input.
lessons.videoQuery: Hugging Face course tokenizers subword algorithms and tokenization pipeline

lessons.title: Embeddings and positions turn identifiers into vectors
lessons.explain: A token identifier is a category, so its numerical magnitude should not imply semantic distance. An embedding table maps each identifier to a learned vector. A sequence becomes a tensor with batch, sequence, and feature dimensions; track those dimensions explicitly to distinguish token positions from features. A model also needs information about order because a collection of token vectors alone does not describe a sentence sequence. Positional representations supply that information in several possible ways. These vectors are learned through an objective and dataset; geometric closeness can be useful, but it does not automatically establish human meaning, fairness, or truth.
lessons.practice: Implement token and learned position embeddings for two short padded sequences. Print the tensor shapes, mask padding where needed, and show that swapping token positions changes the representation.
lessons.deliverable: An embedding worksheet, shape assertions, and a position-swap experiment.
lessons.check: Why should token ID 200 not be treated as twice the meaning of token ID 100?
lessons.answer: Token IDs index arbitrary vocabulary entries. Their arithmetic relationship has no semantic meaning; learned embedding vectors provide task-dependent representations instead.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning word embeddings and positional encoding

lessons.title: Attention is a learned weighted information exchange
lessons.explain: Self-attention lets each sequence position combine information from other permitted positions. Linear maps create queries, keys, and values. Query-key dot products produce scores; scaling and a softmax turn scores into weights, and the weighted values produce the output. For causal prediction, a mask excludes future positions before softmax so training cannot reveal the next token through the input. Multiple heads learn several such projections, followed by other transformations in a transformer block. Compute a tiny example by hand before increasing dimensions. Attention is a mathematical information-mixing operation; a high attention weight is not, by itself, a faithful explanation of an entire model decision.
lessons.practice: Implement one-head scaled dot-product attention on a three-token sequence. Compare to a hand calculation and perturb a future token to test that earlier causal outputs remain unchanged.
lessons.deliverable: Attention code, shape checks, row-sum checks, and a future-token invariance test.
lessons.check: Where must a causal mask be applied, and what failure occurs if future positions remain visible during next-token training?
lessons.answer: Exclude forbidden score positions before normalization, commonly with negative infinity before softmax. Otherwise the model can use future target information and produce misleadingly low training loss without learning a valid causal predictor.
lessons.videoQuery: Dive into Deep Learning scaled dot product attention and transformer masking

lessons.title: Train the next-token objective on a small problem
lessons.explain: Next-token training converts a sequence into input prefixes and the tokens that follow them. The model produces a distribution over its vocabulary at each permitted position, and cross-entropy penalizes assigning low probability to the observed next token. Shift inputs and targets carefully: an off-by-one error can make a convincing training loop solve the wrong task. Teacher forcing supplies observed preceding tokens during training; generation later uses previously generated tokens, so errors can compound. Start with a tiny corpus and model, verify overfitting on one batch, and compare held-out loss with a simple frequency baseline before spending more compute.
lessons.practice: Train a small character-level causal model with a fixed seed and short context. First overfit one batch, then train on a documented split and compare held-out cross-entropy with a unigram baseline.
lessons.deliverable: Training script, input-target alignment test, loss curves, and a baseline comparison.
lessons.check: Can a model with low next-token loss still invent an incorrect factual statement? Explain why.
lessons.answer: Yes. Next-token loss rewards predicting observed text, not verifying claims against reality. Training text can be false or outdated, and the model can generate plausible continuations outside reliable evidence.
lessons.videoQuery: PyTorch language modeling transformer training and cross entropy

lessons.title: Decoding exposes uncertainty and model limits
lessons.explain: At inference, a model offers a probability distribution and a decoding procedure chooses what to emit. Greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token at each step; sampling can vary the output, while temperature changes the sharpness of the sampling distribution. These choices influence repetition, diversity, and error patterns, but they do not convert probability into verified knowledge. Report the exact decoding settings and compare outputs across prompts. A tiny model is an educational instrument, not a general assistant. Finish by connecting failures to corpus coverage, context limits, objective choice, and decoding, while distinguishing measured observations from explanations you have not tested.
lessons.practice: Generate from ten fixed prompts using greedy decoding and two sampling temperatures. Log repetition, invalid continuations, and sensitivity to context; package the model, tests, and an honest limitations report.
lessons.deliverable: A reproducible tiny-language-model project with a decoding comparison and failure analysis.
lessons.check: Does setting temperature to zero make a model truthful or make every provider implementation perfectly repeatable?
lessons.answer: No. Greedy-like decoding selects preferred tokens rather than verifying truth. Provider implementation, floating-point behavior, routing, and version changes may also affect repeatability; record the actual environment and settings.
lessons.videoQuery: Hugging Face generation strategies and language model limitations

workedExample.title: A causal mask defines which information can flow
workedExample.code:
from math import exp
scores = [0.0, 1.0, 8.0, 9.0]
query_position = 1
allowed = scores[:query_position + 1]
maximum = max(allowed)
weights = [exp(s - maximum) for s in allowed]
normalizer = sum(weights)
probabilities = [w / normalizer for w in weights]
probabilities += [0.0] * (len(scores) - len(probabilities))
print([round(p, 3) for p in probabilities])
print("sum", round(sum(probabilities), 6))
workedExample.explanation: The query at position one can attend to positions zero and one, but not future positions two and three. Masking must affect normalization as well as the final displayed weights: the large future scores must not influence the denominator. Subtracting the maximum allowed score stabilizes the exponential calculation without changing the softmax probabilities. A transformer adds learned projections, multiple heads and other layers, but the causal information boundary remains essential when training a next-token model.

assessment.question: Why is zeroing future attention probabilities after an unmasked softmax generally incorrect?
options: Future scores have already affected the normalization denominator.
Softmax can only operate on two values.
Causal attention requires every allowed weight to be equal.
Masking is relevant only at inference time.
assessment.explanation: An unmasked softmax normalizes over all positions. If future scores are included, they affect the probabilities assigned to allowed positions even if their own output weights are later set to zero. Apply the mask before normalization, conventionally by assigning disallowed logits negative infinity. The boundary must hold during training as well as generation to prevent future-information leakage.

connections.before: Autodiff, vector representations and numerical stability combine into sequence modeling.
connections.after: Understanding information flow helps you distinguish a language model’s prediction objective from trustworthy factual answering.

modules.title: Retrieval and grounded generation
modules.summary: Build a retrieval system that can find useful evidence, respect access boundaries, and support answers that are easy to inspect.
modules.why: Generation cannot reliably use information that was never retrieved. Separating retrieval, evidence selection, and answer evaluation makes failures diagnosable.
outcomes: Compare lexical and dense retrieval on labeled queries
Design chunking and indexing with provenance and permissions
Evaluate evidence support and correct abstention separately from fluency

project.title: A handbook assistant with traceable evidence
project.brief: Use a small licensed public handbook or your own synthetic documents. Build search first, then add a constrained answer layer that cites exact passages and can decline unsupported questions.
deliverables: Document inventory with licenses, IDs, and version information
Labeled query set and lexical/dense retrieval comparison
Citation-bearing answers with an abstention policy
Failure analysis covering retrieval, answer support, and access control
rubric: Relevance labels are created before inspecting system outputs where practical
Citations resolve to passages that actually support the answer
Restricted documents cannot enter an unauthorized query context
Unanswerable queries are included in evaluation

pitfalls: Using a vector database before defining retrieval quality
Treating a citation as proof without checking its content
Assuming retrieved document text is trusted instruction

lessons.title: Search quality begins with a query and relevant evidence
lessons.explain: Retrieval selects candidate information for a question; it does not guarantee that the candidates answer it. Begin with a small collection and queries whose relevant passages you can label manually. A lexical baseline such as TF-IDF search often reveals whether the task depends on exact terms, synonyms, or document structure. Measure retrieval against relevance labels using an appropriate ranking metric, and inspect actual misses. A high recall at a large cutoff can still create an unusable context full of noise. Keep the query distribution realistic and separate tuning queries from evaluation queries so retrieval settings do not merely memorize a small benchmark.
lessons.practice: Index twenty short handbook sections with TF-IDF. Write fifteen queries with passage relevance labels before running search, then calculate recall at three and inspect five failures.
lessons.deliverable: A lexical search baseline, labeled queries, metric implementation, and failure examples.
lessons.check: If the answer passage is absent from the retrieved set, can a downstream language model reliably cite that missing evidence?
lessons.answer: No. It may answer from prior knowledge or guess, but it cannot ground the response in an unavailable passage. Retrieval failure must be measured separately from generation behavior.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning retrieval evaluation and information retrieval baselines

lessons.title: Dense vectors provide a second retrieval hypothesis
lessons.explain: Dense retrieval maps queries and passages into vectors whose similarity is intended to reflect relevance under a learned objective. The embedding model, preprocessing, and similarity function are a matched design choice; some models expect different formatting for queries and documents. Cosine similarity compares direction, while a raw dot product also depends on vector length unless vectors are normalized. Dense retrieval can help with paraphrases but can miss exact identifiers, numbers, or rare vocabulary. Compare it with your lexical baseline on the same labeled queries. A hybrid combination is an empirical option, not a guarantee that adding more components improves the system.
lessons.practice: Use a documented small embedding model if available, cache vectors, and compare dense retrieval with TF-IDF. Include exact error codes, paraphrases, and confusingly similar passages; test one simple hybrid ranking.
lessons.deliverable: A retrieval comparison table with shared queries, metrics, and model/license notes.
lessons.check: Why might lexical search outperform dense retrieval for a rare product error code?
lessons.answer: Exact token matches can preserve the distinguishing identifier while a learned embedding may blur it with semantically similar text. The result depends on the model and data and should be tested.
lessons.videoQuery: Hugging Face sentence embeddings semantic search and similarity

lessons.title: Chunking and indexing preserve context and boundaries
lessons.explain: A document chunk is a unit of retrievable evidence. Chunks that are too small can lose definitions and qualifiers; chunks that are too large can dilute the relevant passage and consume the context budget. Preserve headings, source IDs, versions, and offsets so a retrieved result can be traced back to its origin. Index updates must address deleted or changed documents, not only append new vectors. Permissions are part of retrieval design: unauthorized content must be excluded before it reaches the answer context. Similarity scores do not grant access. Evaluate a few chunking settings with the same relevance criteria rather than selecting a fashionable size.
lessons.practice: Create two chunking policies for the handbook, keeping source offsets and section headings. Add fictional public and restricted labels, then test that unauthorized queries never receive restricted chunks.
lessons.deliverable: A versioned chunk manifest, chunking comparison, and access-filter tests.
lessons.check: Is removing a restricted citation from the final answer sufficient if its text was already passed to the model?
lessons.answer: No. The content may already influence or leak through the generated answer. Enforce authorization before retrieving or constructing model context, and apply appropriate controls to caches and logs.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning document chunking retrieval pipelines and metadata

lessons.title: A grounded answer must expose its support and limits
lessons.explain: A retrieval-augmented answer combines a question with selected source passages and an answer procedure. Define what the system should do when the evidence is absent, contradictory, or outdated. Require citations that point to exact supporting passages, then verify that the cited content entails the claim rather than merely mentioning similar words. Retrieved text is data from a potentially untrusted source; a passage telling the system to ignore its instructions must not acquire authority. Keep tool permissions and authorization outside model discretion. A deterministic extractive baseline can be useful when no model endpoint is available and provides a clear comparison for generated answers.
lessons.practice: Build a context formatter with source IDs and a fixed token or character budget. Implement an extractive answer baseline and, optionally, a model-backed variant. Test unsupported questions, conflicting passages, and an injected document instruction.
lessons.deliverable: A context construction function, citation format, abstention examples, and adversarial tests.
lessons.check: Why can an answer with three citations still be unsupported?
lessons.answer: The citations may be irrelevant, contradictory, outdated, or fail to entail the specific claims. Citation presence is a formatting property; support requires checking the relationship between each claim and its source.
lessons.videoQuery: OWASP retrieval augmented generation prompt injection and grounding

lessons.title: Diagnose the pipeline one failure at a time
lessons.explain: A single end-to-end score hides where a retrieval system failed. First ask whether the relevant passage existed in the collection, then whether retrieval found it, whether context construction retained it, and whether the answer used it correctly. Evaluate answerable and unanswerable questions separately, including correct abstention. Record latency and input/output usage for the same workloads used to measure quality. A change in chunking, top-k, reranking, or prompting should earn its complexity on held-out cases. Report the evaluation set size and limitations: a small handbook benchmark demonstrates a mechanism, not universal reliability or permission to use the system in a high-stakes setting.
lessons.practice: Complete a twenty-case evaluation covering answerable, absent, contradictory, stale, and adversarial queries. Classify failures by stage and compare one pipeline change against the baseline under the same context budget.
lessons.deliverable: The handbook assistant, reproducible evaluation report, cost assumptions, and prioritized correction plan.
lessons.check: If increasing top-k improves retrieval recall but lowers answer support, what should you investigate?
lessons.answer: Inspect whether extra passages add contradictory or irrelevant context, crowd out useful evidence, or confuse generation. Compare context selection and answer behavior rather than assuming retrieval recall alone determines end-to-end quality.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning retrieval augmented generation evaluation

workedExample.title: Retrieved text is evidence, not an instruction source
workedExample.explanation: This tiny lexical retriever filters authorization before ranking, returns an identifiable passage and can produce an empty evidence set. A real RAG system needs better retrieval evaluation, document provenance, versioning and reliable authorization, but these boundaries are already visible. An answer must be checked against the actual cited passage; attaching an ID does not make a claim supported. Retrieved text can also contain malicious instructions. Treat it as untrusted data and keep application permissions independent of what the text asks a model to do.

assessment.question: An answer includes a citation to a retrieved document. What has that alone established?
options: That every claim in the answer is supported by the document.
Only that a document was referenced; support must be checked against the actual passage.
That the user is authorized to see every document in the index.
That retrieval recall is 100%.
assessment.explanation: A citation can point to an irrelevant, stale or contradictory passage. Evaluate whether the evidence actually supports each important claim and whether the system should abstain when support is missing. Retrieval quality, answer groundedness and authorization are separate properties. A system can succeed at one while failing at another, so a single attractive example or citation count is insufficient.

connections.before: Nearest-neighbor ideas become an evidence-retrieval system with provenance and permission constraints.
connections.after: LLM evaluation must test missing evidence, wrong evidence, unsupported claims and correct abstention separately.

modules.title: Evaluate language-model behavior and tool use
modules.summary: Turn vague expectations into testable behaviors, then add tools with explicit contracts and controlled authority.
modules.why: A convincing demonstration is weak evidence for a probabilistic system. Evaluation and capability boundaries must be designed before a model is trusted to act.
outcomes: Build a small evaluation set with a rubric and failure taxonomy
Calibrate automated judging against inspected human labels
Implement schema-validated tool calls with explicit permissions and safe failure behavior

project.title: An evaluated assistant with one bounded tool
project.brief: Extend the handbook assistant with a read-only lookup tool over fictional records. Define the permitted behavior, implement a test harness, and compare versions on frozen cases.
deliverables: Behavior specification and labeled evaluation set
Deterministic checks plus a documented judgment rubric
Read-only tool contract and validation tests
Version comparison with disagreements, failures, and uncertainty
rubric: Evaluation covers ordinary, boundary, unsupported, and adversarial inputs
Automated judgments are audited rather than treated as unquestionable truth
Malformed or unauthorized calls cannot execute through the tool layer
Version claims use the same recorded evaluation protocol

pitfalls: Optimizing only for attractive examples
Treating model-based judging as ground truth
Letting a model authorize its own tool permissions

lessons.title: Specify behavior before scoring it
lessons.explain: An assistant can fail in several ways even when its prose sounds helpful: it may answer the wrong question, invent evidence, expose private data, or call an inappropriate tool. Define the allowed behavior and unacceptable failures before choosing a score. Use deterministic tests for properties that have exact answers, such as valid JSON or required fields, and a written rubric for judgments that require interpretation. Keep separate dimensions visible instead of collapsing everything into one attractive number. The evaluation should reflect the intended users, inputs, and decisions. A rubric is a specification that can be challenged, not an objective truth merely because it contains numbers.
lessons.practice: Write a behavior contract for handbook lookup with four scoring dimensions and three unacceptable failures. Create deterministic schema checks and five examples that distinguish formatting correctness from factual support.
lessons.deliverable: A behavior contract, failure taxonomy, rubric, and initial exact checks.
lessons.check: Can syntactically valid JSON be considered a correct answer by itself?
lessons.answer: No. Syntax establishes only that the output can be parsed. The values may be unsupported, incomplete, unauthorized, or inappropriate for the user’s task.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning LLM evaluation specifications and testing

lessons.title: Construct a dataset that can disagree with your intuition
lessons.explain: Evaluation examples determine which failures a system has a chance to reveal. Include common cases, realistic edge cases, and deliberate challenges, while labeling synthetic cases as synthetic rather than claiming population representativeness. Define acceptable answers or evidence requirements before reviewing candidate outputs when practical. If a judgment is ambiguous, record the ambiguity and refine the rubric; a second reviewer can expose disagreements that a single score conceals. Separate development cases from a held-out comparison set, and preserve difficult failures instead of quietly removing them. A small dataset can guide iteration, but its limited coverage and uncertainty must remain visible.
lessons.practice: Create thirty cases grouped by behavior type, reserve ten for final comparison, and label acceptable evidence or abstention. Ask another person to score a subset if available; otherwise repeat a blind self-review later and state the limitation.
lessons.deliverable: Versioned cases, label guidance, a held-out partition, and an agreement/disagreement note.
lessons.check: Why should repeatedly tuning prompts against the final comparison set change how you describe that set?
lessons.answer: Its feedback has influenced model selection, so it is now part of development rather than untouched evaluation. Report the reuse and obtain fresh cases for a stronger final assessment.
lessons.videoQuery: OpenAI evaluation methodology datasets and human review

lessons.title: Automated judges need calibration and attack resistance
lessons.explain: A model-based judge can scale subjective review but introduces another fallible model into the measurement process. Its scores can depend on verbosity, presentation, answer order, prompt wording, or instructions embedded in the answer being judged. Compare its judgments with a manually inspected sample and investigate disagreements before using it to rank systems. For pairwise comparisons, swap answer order and conceal system identity where feasible. Use exact checks for exact properties and retain human review for important ambiguous cases. Report which judge, version, rubric, and settings produced the labels; a judge score is a measurement under assumptions, not direct proof of correctness.
lessons.practice: Implement a judge interface that can use either a human rubric or an optional model endpoint. Audit ten outputs, swap pairwise order, and include one answer that tries to instruct the judge to award full marks.
lessons.deliverable: A judge audit table with agreement, order sensitivity, and injection behavior.
lessons.check: If two systems receive similar judge scores but the judge disagrees with human review on unsupported claims, what should you do?
lessons.answer: Investigate and improve the measurement before declaring equivalence. Separate factual-support checks, refine the rubric, and report uncertainty and disagreement rather than trusting the aggregate score.
lessons.videoQuery: LLM evaluation model as judge limitations calibration and pairwise bias

lessons.title: A tool call is a request through a controlled interface
lessons.explain: A model-generated tool call is untrusted structured input, not authorization to execute arbitrary code. Define a narrow schema, validate types and allowed values, and enforce permissions in ordinary application code. Keep the tool’s capability smaller than the model’s language space: a read-only lookup over permitted records is easier to reason about than a shell command. Tools can time out or return malformed data, so define bounded failures and safe retries. For actions that change state, idempotency and explicit confirmation may be necessary. The model can propose an action; the surrounding system decides whether it is valid, permitted, and safe to perform.
lessons.practice: Implement a read-only lookup tool over fictional records with an allowlisted record ID and field schema. Test malformed JSON, extra fields, unauthorized IDs, timeouts, and an attempted arbitrary command.
lessons.deliverable: A tool contract, validation layer, and automated boundary tests.
lessons.check: Why is a prompt saying “never access unauthorized records” insufficient as the access-control mechanism?
lessons.answer: Model outputs are probabilistic and can be influenced by untrusted inputs. Authorization must be enforced independently by the tool or service using authenticated identity and policy, regardless of what the model requests.
lessons.videoQuery: OWASP excessive agency tool permissions and structured output validation

lessons.title: Compare versions with a release decision you can defend
lessons.explain: A new prompt, model, or tool implementation should be compared under a recorded protocol. Run both versions on the same frozen cases, preserve raw outputs, and inspect paired changes so a small average improvement does not hide a severe regression. Separate quality dimensions, failures with unacceptable consequences, latency, and cost. Repeated trials may be needed for stochastic behavior; report the number of runs and avoid implying precision unsupported by the sample. Define release criteria before seeing the final comparison. A decision can be to keep the simpler baseline, restrict the use case, or gather more evidence rather than automatically adopting the newest model.
lessons.practice: Compare two assistant versions on the held-out cases. Record paired rubric outcomes, schema failures, tool-boundary tests, latency, and estimated usage cost; write a release or no-release decision tied to predefined criteria.
lessons.deliverable: A versioned evaluation harness, raw result archive, regression report, and release rationale.
lessons.check: A version improves mean helpfulness but begins exposing restricted records in one test. Is the average score enough to release it?
lessons.answer: No. An access-control violation breaches a boundary that should be enforced independently of average helpfulness. Fix and retest the boundary, then reassess the release under explicit acceptance criteria.
lessons.videoQuery: Full Stack Deep Learning evaluation driven LLM development

workedExample.title: Schema validity is only the first gate
workedExample.explanation: A well-formed tool request can still be disallowed. This example separates type checking, tool permission and a transaction policy before any side effect. Python booleans are a subclass of int, so the explicit boolean exclusion matters when implementing a strict integer contract by hand. Production systems should use a carefully configured schema validator and server-side authorization, then handle identity, idempotency and audit requirements. Passing these local checks is not a guarantee that a real transaction is authorized to execute.

assessment.question: A language model returns valid JSON matching the tool schema. What should the application do next?
options: Execute it immediately because valid JSON establishes permission.
Trust the retrieved document to decide who has permission.
Apply server-side identity, authorization, policy and side-effect checks before execution.
Hide all errors so the user cannot inspect the action.
assessment.explanation: A schema describes shape and allowed values; it does not establish the caller’s authority or the action’s business validity. The application must enforce permissions and policies outside the model, and consequential actions may require an explicit review step. Treat the model’s output as a proposed action, record what happened, and return bounded, understandable failures rather than silently broadening access.

connections.before: Evaluation criteria become executable boundaries around a language-model application.
connections.after: An agent is safe enough to evaluate only when each tool call retains these independent controls.

modules.title: Reliable agents as bounded state machines
modules.summary: Study when a multi-step agent is useful, then control its state, tools, budgets, and stopping conditions.
modules.why: Autonomy adds failure paths as well as capability. A reliable workflow makes authority, progress, uncertainty, and recovery inspectable.
outcomes: Compare a deterministic workflow with a model-directed loop
Design bounded execution with explicit state and permission checks
Trace multi-step failures and evaluate whether autonomy earns its added cost

project.title: A bounded research-and-draft assistant
project.brief: Build a local assistant that searches a fixed licensed document collection, collects evidence, and drafts a response for human review. Give it no ability to send messages, purchase items, or modify external systems.
deliverables: State diagram and authority map
Deterministic baseline and optional model-directed variant
Bounded runner with timeout, retry, and stop tests
Trace-based evaluation and comparison of quality, cost, and failures
rubric: Every execution has a finite step, time, and tool-use budget
Untrusted documents cannot change permissions or the task objective
State and failures can be reconstructed from redacted traces
The agent variant is compared with a simpler workflow on the same tasks

pitfalls: Calling a loop intelligent without testing task outcomes
Retrying non-idempotent actions blindly
Letting successful intermediate steps conceal an incorrect final result

lessons.title: Start with an explicit workflow before adding autonomy
lessons.explain: A multi-step system maintains state, chooses an action, observes a result, and decides what to do next. In a deterministic workflow, application code specifies those transitions; in a model-directed loop, a model proposes some transitions based on the current context. Both need a clear task objective and a stopping condition. Draw a state machine before choosing a framework so you can see which transitions require judgment and which should remain fixed. If search, select, draft, and validate can be expressed reliably as a short pipeline, that may be the better baseline. Autonomy should earn its complexity through measured benefits on suitable tasks.
lessons.practice: Draw states for receiving a question, retrieving documents, selecting evidence, drafting, checking, and stopping. Implement the deterministic transitions with mocked tools and test every valid and invalid transition.
lessons.deliverable: A state diagram, transition table, and executable deterministic baseline.
lessons.check: What evidence would justify replacing a fixed pipeline with a model-directed loop?
lessons.answer: A representative task set should show that flexible action selection improves required outcomes enough to justify added cost, latency, and failure risk, while remaining within explicit authority and resource limits.
lessons.videoQuery: Anthropic building effective agents workflows versus agents

lessons.title: State is the memory you choose to trust
lessons.explain: An agent’s state should distinguish the user’s task, trusted configuration, tool results, source passages, and model-generated hypotheses. Mixing them into one undifferentiated text blob makes it difficult to preserve authority and diagnose errors. Store structured fields with provenance, and validate updates before accepting them. Summaries reduce context size but can omit qualifications or accidentally promote an uncertain claim into a fact; retain links to original evidence. Retrieved text and tool output remain untrusted data even when they look like instructions. The application, not a passage or a model’s guess, determines which state changes and actions are permitted.
lessons.practice: Define a typed state object containing objective, allowed tools, evidence IDs, hypotheses, remaining budget, and status. Test that a retrieved passage cannot overwrite the objective or grant a new tool permission.
lessons.deliverable: A state schema, validated update function, and provenance-preservation tests.
lessons.check: Why should a model-written summary not silently replace all original evidence in a research workflow?
lessons.answer: A summary can omit context or introduce errors. Keeping source references and the ability to inspect originals allows claims to be checked and prevents accumulated summaries from becoming unsupported authority.
lessons.videoQuery: OWASP prompt injection untrusted context and agent memory boundaries

lessons.title: Bound every loop and make retries deliberate
lessons.explain: A system that can repeatedly plan and call tools needs resource limits independent of the model’s willingness to stop. Set maximum steps, wall-clock time, tool calls, and token or cost budgets, and define the outcome when any limit is reached. Retry only failures that are plausibly transient, with bounded attempts and a delay policy; repeated invalid requests need correction rather than blind repetition. An idempotent action can be repeated without changing its effect beyond the first successful execution, which matters when a timeout hides whether an operation completed. Start with read-only tools and make termination and recovery visible in the state machine.
lessons.practice: Add step, elapsed-time, and tool-call limits to the runner. Inject a hanging tool, repeated invalid arguments, and a transient read failure; verify bounded termination and a useful final status.
lessons.deliverable: A bounded execution runner and failure-injection tests with recorded stopping reasons.
lessons.check: Why can retrying a payment request after a timeout create a different risk from retrying a read-only search?
lessons.answer: The payment may already have succeeded even though the response was lost. A retry can duplicate the side effect unless the service uses an appropriate idempotency mechanism and authorization; a read-only search ordinarily has no equivalent state change.
lessons.videoQuery: Reliable agent orchestration timeouts retries and idempotency

lessons.title: Trace decisions without leaking private data
lessons.explain: A final answer reveals little about a multi-step failure. Record structured events such as state transition, tool name, validated arguments, status, duration, and evidence IDs so the execution can be reconstructed. Redact secrets and unnecessary personal data, and define retention rather than logging everything by default. Distinguish planning errors, retrieval misses, invalid tool requests, infrastructure failures, and unsupported conclusions. A trace can suggest a cause, but a controlled replay or targeted test provides stronger evidence. Do not rely on a model’s self-description as a faithful account of its internal reasoning; inspect observable actions and their consequences instead.
lessons.practice: Create a structured event log for five successful and five deliberately failed tasks. Redact a synthetic secret field, reconstruct one failure from the trace, and write a targeted regression test.
lessons.deliverable: A redacted trace format, failure taxonomy, replay example, and regression test.
lessons.check: Is a model’s explanation of why it chose a tool sufficient to establish the actual cause of a failure?
lessons.answer: No. Such explanations can be incomplete or post hoc. Use observable state, tool requests, results, and controlled tests to support causal conclusions.
